Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Section 2(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, the statutory term "assessment" includes which of the following?
OptionA: Only the determination of duty payable on imported goods
OptionB: Only re-assessment ordered by appellate authorities
OptionC: Only the physical examination and classification of goods
OptionD: Provisional assessment, self-assessment, re-assessment and any assessment where duty is assessed as nil
Explanation: Section 2(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 defines "assessment" broadly to include provisional assessment, self-assessment, re-assessment, and any order of assessment in which the duty assessed is nil. (Source: Bare Act & R.K. Jain Customs Law Manual)
CorrectText: Provisional assessment, self-assessment, re-assessment and any assessment where duty is assessed as nil
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 2(2)

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Section 2(24) of the Customs Act, 1962, "imported goods" cease to be imported goods when:
OptionA: They are cleared for home consumption
OptionB: They are deposited into a public bonded warehouse
OptionC: They are unloaded at the customs port or airport
OptionD: They cross the territorial waters of India
Explanation: Under Section 2(24), "imported goods" means any goods brought into India from a place outside India but does not include goods which have been cleared for home consumption. Once out of charge for home consumption is granted, they lose their imported character. (Source: CBIC / Section 2(24))
CorrectText: They are cleared for home consumption
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 2(24)

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: How does Section 2(33) of the Customs Act, 1962 define "prohibited goods"?
OptionA: Any goods completely banned from trade under Indian penal statutes only
OptionB: Goods imported without an Importer-Exporter Code (IEC)
OptionC: Only narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances
OptionD: Any goods the import or export of which is subject to any prohibition under this Act or any other law, but does not include goods where conditions have been satisfied
Explanation: Section 2(33) defines prohibited goods as goods whose import or export is prohibited under the Customs Act or any other law for the time being in force, but expressly excludes goods in respect of which the conditions of import/export have been complied with. (Source: Section 2(33) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Any goods the import or export of which is subject to any prohibition under this Act or any other law, but does not include goods where conditions have been satisfied
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 2(33)

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Section 7 of the Customs Act, 1962, the statutory authority empowered to appoint customs ports, customs airports, and Inland Container Depots (ICDs) is:
OptionA: The Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT)
OptionB: The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways directly
OptionC: The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), by notification in the Official Gazette
OptionD: The State Government having maritime jurisdiction
Explanation: Under Section 7(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, the Board (CBIC) is empowered, by notification in the Official Gazette, to appoint customs ports, airports, inland container depots (ICDs), and land customs stations. (Source: CBIC / Section 7)
CorrectText: The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), by notification in the Official Gazette
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 7

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Which section of the Customs Act, 1962 operates as the primary charging section for the levy of customs duties on goods?
Explanation: Section 12 is the charging section of the Customs Act, 1962. It provides that duties of customs shall be levied at specified rates on goods imported into, or exported from, India, as provided under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 or other applicable laws. (Source: R.K. Jain Customs Law Manual)
CorrectText: Section 12
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 12

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1962, if imported goods are pilfered after unloading thereof and before an order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse:
OptionA: Duty is abated in proportion to the value of remaining cargo
OptionB: The importer must pay duty but can claim full refund within 30 days
OptionC: The importer is not liable to pay duty, and under Section 45(3) the custodian is liable to pay duty
OptionD: The shipping line must pay double the duty assessed
Explanation: Under Section 13, the importer is completely exonerated from paying duty on pilfered goods. Furthermore, under Section 45(3), the custodian of the goods is statutorily liable to pay duty on such pilfered goods. Section 13 does not apply if goods are restored or if pilferage occurs after clearance. (Source: Section 13 & Section 45(3) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The importer is not liable to pay duty, and under Section 45(3) the custodian is liable to pay duty
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 13

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 15(1)(a) of the Customs Act, 1962, the rate of duty and tariff valuation applicable to imported goods cleared for home consumption under Section 46 shall be the rate in force on:
OptionA: The date of payment of duty in the bank
OptionB: The date on which the goods are physically examined at the dock
OptionC: The date of sailing from the load port abroad
OptionD: The date of presentation of the Bill of Entry or the date of entry inwards of the vessel, whichever is later
Explanation: Section 15(1)(a) mandates that for goods entered for home consumption, the relevant rate of duty and tariff valuation is that in force on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry, or the date of arrival/entry inwards of the conveyance, whichever is later. (Source: CBIC / Section 15(1)(a))
CorrectText: The date of presentation of the Bill of Entry or the date of entry inwards of the vessel, whichever is later
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 15(1)(a)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 15(1)(b) of the Customs Act, 1962, the relevant date for determining the rate of duty on goods cleared from a bonded warehouse for home consumption is:
OptionA: The date of filing of the Into-Bond Bill of Entry (Space / Yellow Bill)
OptionB: The date of deposit of goods into the warehouse
OptionC: The date on which the Ex-Bond Bill of Entry for home consumption is presented under Section 68
OptionD: The date when the warehousing period of 1 year expires
Explanation: Section 15(1)(b) provides that in the case of warehoused goods cleared for home consumption under Section 68, the rate of duty and tariff valuation is that in force on the date on which a Bill of Entry for home consumption in respect of such goods is presented. (Source: Section 15(1)(b) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The date on which the Ex-Bond Bill of Entry for home consumption is presented under Section 68
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 15(1)(b)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 16(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, the rate of duty and tariff valuation applicable to export goods entered under a Shipping Bill shall be the rate in force on:
OptionA: The date on which foreign exchange proceeds are realized
OptionB: The date on which the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading (Let Export Order) under Section 51
OptionC: The date of issuance of the Mate Receipt by the ship master
OptionD: The date of filing the Shipping Bill electronically on ICEGATE
Explanation: Under Section 16(1)(a), the rate of duty for export goods is the rate in force on the date on which the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading of the goods (Let Export Order) under Section 51. (Source: Section 16(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The date on which the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading (Let Export Order) under Section 51
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 16(1)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 17 of the Customs Act, 1962, how is the primary assessment of duty conducted on imported or export goods?
OptionA: Assessment conducted exclusively by the Custodian
OptionB: Compulsory assessment by the Assistant Commissioner in every case
OptionC: Provisional assessment with mandatory bank guarantee
OptionD: Self-assessment by the importer or exporter, subject to verification by the Proper Officer via Risk Management System (RMS)
Explanation: Section 17(1) establishes the regime of self-assessment whereby the importer or exporter self-assesses duty. Under Section 17(2), the proper officer may verify the self-assessment, selecting entries based on risk evaluation criteria (RMS). (Source: Section 17 Customs Act, 1962 / CBIC Circulars)
CorrectText: Self-assessment by the importer or exporter, subject to verification by the Proper Officer via Risk Management System (RMS)
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 17

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Which of the following is a valid statutory ground for ordering a Provisional Assessment under Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1962?
OptionA: The goods are banned under the Foreign Trade Policy
OptionB: The importer requests extra time to pay assessed duty without interest
OptionC: Chemical or other tests are required, or further inquiry/documents are necessary, or valuation cannot be immediately determined
OptionD: The Customs Broker forgot to sign the digital declaration
Explanation: Section 18(1) permits provisional assessment where chemical/other tests are pending, where the importer/exporter has not produced necessary documents, or where the proper officer deems it necessary to make further inquiry to determine duty or valuation, subject to execution of a bond. (Source: Section 18 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Chemical or other tests are required, or further inquiry/documents are necessary, or valuation cannot be immediately determined
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 18

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 23(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, remission of duty on imported goods is permissible where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner that goods have been:
OptionA: Lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption
OptionB: Pilfered while stored in a private bonded warehouse
OptionC: Cleared without physical examination by mistake
OptionD: Exported without payment of IGST under LUT
Explanation: Section 23(1) governs remission where goods are lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed (such as by accidental fire, flood, or natural disaster) at any time before clearance for home consumption. (Source: Section 23(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 23(1)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 23(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, an owner may relinquish title to imported goods and avoid payment of duty thereon, provided:
OptionA: The importer pays a mandatory penalty of 25% of the cargo value
OptionB: The goods have already been taken out of customs custody
OptionC: Relinquishment is done within 1 year from the date of import manifest
OptionD: Relinquishment is made before an order for clearance for home consumption (Sec 47) or deposit in warehouse (Sec 60), and no offence appears to have been committed
Explanation: Section 23(2) allows the owner of imported goods to relinquish title before an order for clearance for home consumption under Section 47 or deposit in warehouse under Section 60, whereupon duty liability ceases, provided no offence has been committed in respect of such goods. (Source: Section 23(2) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Relinquishment is made before an order for clearance for home consumption (Sec 47) or deposit in warehouse (Sec 60), and no offence appears to have been committed
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 23(2)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 22 of the Customs Act, 1962, how is duty abated on imported goods that have been damaged or deteriorated before or during unloading?
OptionA: Duty is reduced to a flat 5% ad valorem
OptionB: Duty is completely waived and goods are returned to exporter
OptionC: Abatement is granted only if damage exceeds 75% of invoice value
OptionD: Duty is abated in proportion to the diminution in the value of the goods (Duty = Full Duty x Value after damage / Value before damage)
Explanation: Under Section 22(1) & 22(2), duty on damaged/deteriorated goods is charged in proportion to the reduced value: Duty Payable = Full Duty on sound goods x (Value of damaged goods / Value of sound goods). (Source: Section 22 Customs Act, 1962 / R.K. Jain)
CorrectText: Duty is abated in proportion to the diminution in the value of the goods (Duty = Full Duty x Value after damage / Value before damage)
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 22

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the standard limitation period for filing an application for refund of customs duty paid by an individual or importer?
OptionA: 3 years from the end of the financial year
OptionB: 1 year from the date of payment of duty or interest
OptionC: 30 days from the date of final assessment
OptionD: 6 months from the date of clearance
Explanation: Under Section 27(1), any person claiming refund of duty or interest paid must make an application before the expiry of 1 year from the date of payment of such duty or interest, subject to the doctrine of unjust enrichment under Section 27(2). (Source: Section 27 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 1 year from the date of payment of duty or interest
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 27

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962, what are the respective statutory time limits for issuing a Show Cause Notice (SCN) for recovery of duty in normal cases versus cases involving collusion, wilful misstatement, or suppression of facts?
Explanation: Under Section 28, the proper officer can serve an SCN within 2 years from the relevant date in normal cases (amended by Finance Act 2016), and within 5 years where duty was not levied/short-levied by reason of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. (Source: Section 28 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Normal: 2 years; Fraud/Suppression: 5 years
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 28AA of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the notified annual rate of interest payable on delayed payment of customs duty?
Explanation: Notification No. 33/2016-Customs (N.T.) notified the rate of interest under Section 28AA at 15% per annum for delayed payment of customs duty. (Source: CBIC / Section 28AA)
CorrectText: 15% per annum
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28AA

Chapter: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests
Question: Under Section 30 of the Customs Act, 1962, an Arrival Manifest or Import Manifest (IGM) in respect of a vessel or aircraft carrying imported goods must be delivered electronically:
OptionA: Within 24 hours after anchoring at the berth
OptionB: At the discretion of the master before port clearance
OptionC: Within 7 days of completion of discharge
OptionD: Prior to the arrival of the vessel or aircraft at the customs port or airport
Explanation: Section 30(1) requires the person-in-charge of a vessel or aircraft to deliver an electronic arrival manifest/import report prior to the arrival of the conveyance, in the prescribed form. (Source: Section 30 Customs Act, 1962 / Sea Cargo Manifest Regs)
CorrectText: Prior to the arrival of the vessel or aircraft at the customs port or airport
Topic: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests — Section 30

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962, an importer is required to present a Bill of Entry before the end of the next day following the day of arrival of the conveyance. If filed late without approved cause, what late fee is leviable?
OptionA: Rs 5,000 per day for the initial three days, and Rs 10,000 per day for each subsequent day of delay
OptionB: Flat 1% of the assessable value per day
OptionC: Rs 2,500 per day up to a maximum of Rs 25,000
Explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 46(3) read with Bill of Entry Regulations, late presentation charges are Rs 5,000 per day for the first three days, and Rs 10,000 per day for each subsequent day of delay. (Source: CBIC Circular No. 12/2017-Cus & Section 46(3))
CorrectText: Rs 5,000 per day for the initial three days, and Rs 10,000 per day for each subsequent day of delay
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 46(3)

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Section 47(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, once an electronic Bill of Entry is returned to the importer for payment of duty, the importer must pay the assessed duty within:
OptionA: 48 hours from arrival of the vessel
OptionB: The same day or by the next day (excluding holidays) of return of the Bill of Entry, failing which interest at 15% is payable
Explanation: Section 47(2) mandates that the importer shall pay the duty within the same day or by the next day (excluding holidays) of the date on which the Bill of Entry is returned to him for payment. Delay attracts interest under Section 28AA. (Source: Section 47(2) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The same day or by the next day (excluding holidays) of return of the Bill of Entry, failing which interest at 15% is payable
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 47(2)

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Section 48 of the Customs Act, 1962, if imported goods are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused within what time period from unloading may the custodian, after notice, sell them with customs permission?
Explanation: Section 48 provides that if any goods brought into India are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped within 30 days from the date of unloading (or extended period), the person having custody may, after notice to the importer and with permission of customs, sell them. (Source: Section 48 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 30 days
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 48

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 58A of the Customs Act, 1962, what is a "Special Warehouse"?
OptionA: A warehouse licensed for storing notified goods (e.g. duty-free shops, ship stores, crude petroleum) under the physical lock and key of customs
OptionC: A transit shed operated by the Port Authority
OptionD: A private warehouse licensed for non-dutiable cargo
Explanation: Section 58A empowers the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner to license a special warehouse wherein physical lock and custody of customs is maintained. Goods notified under Sec 58A include duty-free shop goods, supply to foreign-going vessels/aircrafts, and specified sensitive goods. (Source: Section 58A Customs Act, 1962 / CBIC)
CorrectText: A warehouse licensed for storing notified goods (e.g. duty-free shops, ship stores, crude petroleum) under the physical lock and key of customs
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 58A

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 59(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the monetary liability of the warehousing bond executed by an importer before warehousing goods?
OptionA: A sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed on such goods
OptionB: Equal to the assessable CIF value of the goods
OptionC: Twice the basic customs duty only
OptionD: Equal to the duty plus 18% interest
Explanation: Section 59(1) mandates the execution of a bond binding the importer in a sum equal to thrice the amount of duty assessed on the goods, undertaking to observe all warehousing rules and pay duty, interest, and penalties. (Source: Section 59(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: A sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed on such goods
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 59

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 61 of the Customs Act, 1962, for how long may goods (other than capital goods for EOUs / MOOWR) remain warehoused without interest on duty becoming payable?
OptionD: 90 days from the date of deposit in warehouse
Explanation: Section 61(2) specifies that where warehoused goods remain in a warehouse beyond a period of 90 days from the date of deposit, interest at the notified rate (15% p.a.) is payable on the duty from the expiry of the said 90 days till clearance. (Source: Section 61(2) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 90 days from the date of deposit in warehouse
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 61

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: The MOOWR Scheme (Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations) is framed under which section of the Customs Act, 1962?
Explanation: Section 65 allows manufacture and other operations in a bonded warehouse with permission. Under the revamped MOOWR regulations, imported capital goods and raw materials enjoy duty deferment until cleared into DTA or duty exemption if exported. (Source: Section 65 Customs Act, 1962 / MOOWR Regs 2019)
CorrectText: Section 65
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 65

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962, statements recorded during summons before a Gazetted Officer of Customs:
OptionA: Expire after 30 days if an FIR is not registered
OptionB: Can only be taken in the presence of the examinee's advocate as a matter of absolute right
OptionC: Are inadmissible hearsay evidence in any court of law
OptionD: Are deemed to be recorded in a judicial proceeding within the meaning of Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code
Explanation: Section 108(4) provides that all persons summoned are bound to state the truth, and an inquiry under Section 108 is deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of Section 193 and Section 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). (Source: Section 108 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Are deemed to be recorded in a judicial proceeding within the meaning of Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 108

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Section 114A of the Customs Act, 1962 prescribes a mandatory equal penalty (100% of duty and interest) in which category of contraventions?
OptionA: Baggage declarations with valuation errors below Rs 5,000
OptionB: Short-levy or non-levy of duty or erroneous refund by reason of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts
OptionC: Technical errors in digital signature certificates on ICEGATE
OptionD: Every procedural delay in filing Bill of Entry
Explanation: Section 114A imposes a mandatory penalty equal to the duty or interest not levied, short-levied or erroneously refunded where such non-levy is by reason of collusion or any wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. If paid within 30 days with duty and interest, penalty is reduced to 25%. (Source: Section 114A Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Short-levy or non-levy of duty or erroneous refund by reason of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114A

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: What is the maximum penalty leviable under Section 114AA of the Customs Act, 1962 for knowingly using false and incorrect material or declarations?
OptionB: Up to five times the value of the goods
OptionD: Up to double the assessable value
Explanation: Section 114AA penalizes intentional use of false or incorrect declarations, statements or documents with a penalty up to five times the value of the goods (specifically enacted to combat invoice fraud and fraudulent export claims). (Source: Section 114AA Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Up to five times the value of the goods
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114AA

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 125 of the Customs Act, 1962, when goods are confiscated, the adjudicating officer may give an option to pay a redemption fine in lieu of confiscation. What is the statutory ceiling on such fine?
OptionA: There is no ceiling; it is at absolute discretion of the officer
OptionB: It shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less the duty chargeable thereon
OptionC: It cannot exceed the Basic Customs Duty
OptionD: It cannot exceed 25% of the CIF value
Explanation: The proviso to Section 125(1) stipulates that the fine in lieu of confiscation shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less the duty chargeable thereon. (Source: Section 125 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: It shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less the duty chargeable thereon
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 125

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: What is the statutory time limit for filing an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 128, and what is the mandatory pre-deposit required under Section 129E?
OptionC: 60 days (extendable by 30 days on sufficient cause); mandatory pre-deposit of 7.5% of duty demanded or penalty
Explanation: Section 128(1) allows 60 days to appeal to Commissioner (Appeals), with 30 days condonation power. Section 129E mandates a pre-deposit of 7.5% of duty demanded or penalty imposed for maintaining the appeal before Commissioner (Appeals). (Source: Section 128 & 129E Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 60 days (extendable by 30 days on sufficient cause); mandatory pre-deposit of 7.5% of duty demanded or penalty
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 128 & Section 129E

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 129A of the Customs Act, 1962, which of the following matters decided by a Commissioner (Appeals) is specifically EXCLUDED from the appellate jurisdiction of CESTAT (and goes to Central Government revision under Sec 129DD)?
OptionA: Valuation of chemical inputs under CVR 2007
OptionD: Baggage, drawback, and shortage of goods in conveyances
Explanation: The first proviso to Section 129A(1) excludes orders passed by Commissioner (Appeals) relating to (a) loss of goods/shortage in conveyance, (b) baggage, and (c) drawback under Chapter X. These are reviewable by the Central Government under Section 129DD Revision. (Source: Section 129A Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Baggage, drawback, and shortage of goods in conveyances
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129A

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 135 of the Customs Act, 1962, in cases of duty evasion or fraudulent evasion of prohibitions where the value/duty involved exceeds Rs 50 Lakhs, the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to:
Explanation: Section 135(1)(i) provides that in cases of goods involving duty evasion exceeding Rs 50 Lakhs, or prohibited goods under Section 11, the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 7 years and with fine. (Source: Section 135 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 7 years and with fine
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 135

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, on what base value is Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) calculated on imported goods?
OptionA: Assessable Value (CIF) plus Basic Customs Duty (BCD) plus any other applicable customs duties/cesses (except IGST and GST Cess)
Explanation: Under Section 3(8) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, the value for levying IGST under Section 3(7) is the assessable value determined under Section 14 plus Basic Customs Duty and all other duties of customs leviable, excluding IGST and GST Compensation Cess. (Source: Section 3(7)/(8) CTA 1975)
CorrectText: Assessable Value (CIF) plus Basic Customs Duty (BCD) plus any other applicable customs duties/cesses (except IGST and GST Cess)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Section 3(7)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Section 9A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, what is Anti-Dumping Duty and what is its statutory validity duration unless revoked earlier?
OptionA: A penalty levied by the Port Trust on unexamined containers
OptionB: A duty equal to the margin of dumping (Normal Value minus Export Price) to offset market injury, remaining in force for 5 years from notification
OptionC: A duty on export of raw materials valid for 1 year
OptionD: A permanent non-expiring duty on all Chinese products
Explanation: Under Section 9A(1) & 9A(5), Anti-Dumping Duty is levied to counteract dumping (margin = Normal Value in exporting country minus Export Price). It ceases to have effect on the expiry of 5 years from the date of imposition, unless extended via sunset review. (Source: Section 9A CTA 1975)
CorrectText: A duty equal to the margin of dumping (Normal Value minus Export Price) to offset market injury, remaining in force for 5 years from notification
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Section 9A

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: According to General Interpretative Rule (GIR) 1 of the Import Tariff, titles of Sections, Chapters, and Sub-Chapters:
OptionA: Are provided for ease of reference only, and legal classification is determined strictly according to the terms of the headings and relative Section/Chapter Notes
OptionB: Have overriding statutory force over Chapter Notes
OptionC: Can be ignored if the Customs Broker prefers another classification
OptionD: Are binding only in anti-dumping investigations
Explanation: GIR 1 establishes that titles are for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes. (Source: GIR Rule 1 / R.K. Jain Customs Tariff)
CorrectText: Are provided for ease of reference only, and legal classification is determined strictly according to the terms of the headings and relative Section/Chapter Notes
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 1

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under GIR Rule 2(a), how are incomplete, unfinished, or unassembled/disassembled articles (such as CKD/SKD kits) classified?
OptionA: Under the heading of the complete or finished article, provided as presented they have the essential character of the complete or finished article
OptionB: Always as miscellaneous parts under Chapter 98
OptionC: They must be classified piece by piece under separate tariff lines
OptionD: Under the heading of raw steel or plastic according to weight
Explanation: GIR 2(a) provides that any reference to an article shall be taken to include an incomplete or unfinished article, provided it has the essential character of the complete article; it also applies to complete articles presented unassembled or disassembled (CKD/SKD). (Source: GIR Rule 2(a))
CorrectText: Under the heading of the complete or finished article, provided as presented they have the essential character of the complete or finished article
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 2(a)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under GIR Rule 3(a), when goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, which rule of precedence applies?
OptionA: Alphabetical order of the tariff description
OptionB: The heading with the highest basic customs duty rate
OptionC: The heading that appears first in numerical order
OptionD: The heading providing a more specific description is preferred over headings providing a more general description
Explanation: GIR 3(a) states that the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description (e.g. electric shavers under 85.10 rather than electro-mechanical domestic appliances under 85.09). (Source: GIR Rule 3(a))
CorrectText: The heading providing a more specific description is preferred over headings providing a more general description
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 3(a)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: When goods cannot be classified by reference to GIR Rule 3(a) (specific description) or GIR Rule 3(b) (essential character), how are they classified under GIR Rule 3(c)?
OptionA: Under the heading with the lowest combined tax rate
OptionB: Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
OptionD: Under the heading chosen by the importer
Explanation: GIR 3(c) mandates that when goods cannot be classified by 3(a) or 3(b), they shall be classified under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration. (Source: GIR Rule 3(c))
CorrectText: Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 3(c)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under GIR Rule 5(a), camera cases, musical instrument cases, and specially fitted containers presented with the articles they are intended for:
OptionA: Are classified with such articles if specially shaped/fitted, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles, unless the container gives the whole its essential character
OptionB: Are always completely exempt from customs duty
OptionC: Must be classified separately under Chapter 42 in all circumstances
OptionD: Are classified under the container's own raw material heading
Explanation: GIR 5(a) provides that specially shaped/fitted containers suitable for long-term use (e.g. violin case, camera case) presented with the articles are classified with those articles, unless the container imparts the essential character to the whole. (Source: GIR Rule 5(a))
CorrectText: Are classified with such articles if specially shaped/fitted, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles, unless the container gives the whole its essential character
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 5(a)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 10(1)(a)(i) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007, which category of commission is specifically EXCLUDED from being added to the transaction value?
OptionA: Brokerage paid to a freight forwarder
OptionB: Royalties and license fees paid as a condition of sale
OptionC: Buying commissions paid by the buyer to his purchasing agent abroad
OptionD: Selling commissions paid to foreign brokers
Explanation: Rule 10(1)(a)(i) explicitly mandates the addition of commissions and brokerage, "except buying commissions". A buying commission paid by an importer to his agent for representation abroad does not form part of the assessable value. (Source: Rule 10(1) CVR 2007 / CBIC)
CorrectText: Buying commissions paid by the buyer to his purchasing agent abroad
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3 & Rule 10(1)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 10(2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, where the actual cost of transport and insurance from the port of shipment to India are not ascertainable, what statutory percentages of FOB value apply?
OptionA: Transport: 15% of FOB; Insurance: 1% of FOB
OptionB: Transport: 25% of FOB; Insurance: 0.5% of FOB
OptionD: Transport: 20% of FOB; Insurance: 1.125% of FOB
Explanation: Under Rule 10(2), if sea/air freight is not ascertainable, it is taken as 20% of FOB. If insurance is not ascertainable, it is computed at 1.125% of FOB. (Note: 1% landing charges were omitted in 2017). (Source: Rule 10(2) CVR 2007 / Notification 91/2017-Cus (N.T.))
CorrectText: Transport: 20% of FOB; Insurance: 1.125% of FOB
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what is the sequence between Rule 7 (Deductive Value) and Rule 8 (Computed Value)?
OptionA: The order of application of Rule 7 and Rule 8 can be reversed at the request of the importer and with the approval of the Proper Officer
OptionB: Rule 7 applies only to related party transactions
OptionC: Neither rule can be applied unless CESTAT gives prior sanction
Explanation: The proviso to Rule 3(4) of CVR 2007 explicitly states that at the request of the importer and with the approval of the proper officer, the order of application of rules 7 and 8 may be reversed. (Source: CVR 2007 / CBIC)
CorrectText: The order of application of Rule 7 and Rule 8 can be reversed at the request of the importer and with the approval of the Proper Officer
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 7 & Rule 8

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 12 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, when the Proper Officer has reasonable doubt as to the truth or accuracy of the declared value, he must:
OptionA: Immediately seize the goods without hearing
OptionB: Call for further information/evidence, and if doubt persists, inform the grounds to the importer in writing and provide an opportunity of being heard before rejecting transaction value
OptionC: Refer the matter to the Directorate General of Valuation within 24 hours
OptionD: Directly double the assessable value under the residual method
Explanation: Rule 12 prescribes the procedure for rejection of declared value: the officer asks for documents/explanation, and if reasonable doubt persists, gives grounds in writing and provides a reasonable opportunity of being heard before proceeding to sequential valuation methods. (Source: Rule 12 CVR 2007 / R.K. Jain)
CorrectText: Call for further information/evidence, and if doubt persists, inform the grounds to the importer in writing and provide an opportunity of being heard before rejecting transaction value
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 12

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Section 11(2) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992, what is the maximum statutory penalty for contravening the provisions of the Act, Rules, or Foreign Trade Policy?
OptionA: Suspension of driving license of the exporter
OptionB: Not less than Rs 10,000 and not exceeding five times the value of the goods or services or technology in respect of which contravention is made
Explanation: Section 11(2) of the FTDR Act, 1992 prescribes that the penalty shall not be less than Rs 10,000 and not exceed five times the value of the goods, services, or technology in respect of which the contravention has been made or attempted. (Source: Section 11 FTDR Act, 1992)
CorrectText: Not less than Rs 10,000 and not exceeding five times the value of the goods or services or technology in respect of which contravention is made
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 7 & Section 11

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: What is the unique policy duration feature introduced in the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023 compared to earlier Foreign Trade Policies?
OptionA: It is dynamic and open-ended with no end date, subject to continuous updates as per global trade dynamics
OptionB: It applies only to export of agricultural items
OptionC: It requires annual parliamentary re-enactment every April
OptionD: It has a strict 3-year sunset clause
Explanation: FTP 2023 departed from the traditional 5-year fixed cycle; it is an open-ended, dynamic policy document designed to be updated continuously based on feedback and global economic trends. (Source: DGFT / FTP 2023 Preamble)
CorrectText: It is dynamic and open-ended with no end date, subject to continuous updates as per global trade dynamics
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Chapter 1 — Legal Framework

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Chapter 4 of FTP 2023, what is the minimum value addition generally prescribed for exports under the Advance Authorisation Scheme, and what are the standard validity periods for import and export obligation?
OptionA: Value Addition: 33%; Import: 6 months; Export Obligation: 12 months
OptionB: Value Addition: 15% (except tea 50%); Import Validity: 12 months; Export Obligation Period: 18 months
OptionC: Value Addition: 50%; Import: 18 months; Export Obligation: 24 months
OptionD: Value Addition: 5%; Import: 24 months; Export Obligation: 36 months
Explanation: Under Paragraph 4.09 of FTP 2023, the minimum value addition is 15% (except for tea where it is 50%). Validity for import is 12 months from the date of issue, and the standard Export Obligation Period (EOP) is 18 months. (Source: FTP 2023 & HBP Para 4.09/4.40)
CorrectText: Value Addition: 15% (except tea 50%); Import Validity: 12 months; Export Obligation Period: 18 months
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Advance Authorisation Scheme

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Chapter 4 of FTP 2023, what is the minimum value addition required for Duty Free Import Authorisation (DFIA), and can the DFIA be transferred to other parties?
OptionA: Minimum 15% value addition; transferable immediately on issuance
OptionB: Minimum 20% value addition; transferable after the export obligation has been discharged and endorsement made by DGFT
OptionC: Minimum 50% value addition; transferable only to SEZ units
Explanation: Paragraph 4.25 of FTP 2023 requires a minimum value addition of 20% for DFIA. Once export obligation is fulfilled and export proceeds are realized, the DFIA and/or imported materials are freely transferable. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 4.25 / 4.27)
CorrectText: Minimum 20% value addition; transferable after the export obligation has been discharged and endorsement made by DGFT
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — DFIA Scheme

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under the Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) Scheme in FTP 2023, what is the export obligation requirement for capital goods imported at zero customs duty?
OptionA: Equal to the CIF value of capital goods within 3 years
OptionB: Export obligation equal to 8 times the FOB value in 8 years
OptionC: Export obligation equivalent to 6 times of duty saved on capital goods, to be fulfilled in 6 years from authorization date, while maintaining average export turnover
OptionD: Equal to 2 times the duty saved, with no turnover condition
Explanation: Paragraph 5.01 of FTP 2023 provides that capital goods can be imported at zero customs duty under EPCG, subject to an export obligation equivalent to 6 times the duties, taxes and cesses saved, to be fulfilled within 6 years, over and above maintaining the average export performance. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 5.01)
CorrectText: Export obligation equivalent to 6 times of duty saved on capital goods, to be fulfilled in 6 years from authorization date, while maintaining average export turnover
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Chapter 5 — EPCG Scheme

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: What special concession in Export Obligation is granted under the EPCG Scheme of FTP 2023 for units manufacturing green technology products (e.g. solar cells, EV vehicles, rainwater harvesting)?
OptionB: Full cash subsidy of 50% of machine value
OptionC: Export obligation period is extended to 15 years
OptionD: Capital goods can be sold in DTA without any export obligation
Explanation: Under Paragraph 5.11 of FTP 2023, for exporters manufacturing green technology products (like solar power, wind turbines, electric vehicles), the export obligation is reduced by 25% (i.e. EO is 75% of normal EO). (Source: FTP 2023 Para 5.11)
CorrectText: Export obligation is reduced by 25%
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Green Technology Concession

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: What are the revised export performance thresholds (in FOB US$ million over the current plus 3 preceding financial years) for 1-Star to 5-Star Export Houses under FTP 2023?
Explanation: FTP 2023 rationalized the Status Holder export thresholds: One Star ($3 Million), Two Star ($15 Million), Three Star ($50 Million), Four Star ($200 Million), and Five Star ($800 Million). Double weightage is given to MSMEs and women entrepreneurs. (Source: FTP 2023 Table 1.3)
CorrectText: 1-Star: $3M; 2-Star: $15M; 3-Star: $50M; 4-Star: $200M; 5-Star: $800M
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Chapter 1 — Status Recognition

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Which of the following is an authorized operational privilege granted to Status Holders under FTP 2023?
OptionA: Authorization to self-certify Certificate of Origin (non-preferential) and exemption from furnishing Bank Guarantee under FTP duty exemption schemes
OptionB: Exemption from payment of GST on domestic sales
OptionC: Right to retain 100% foreign exchange in cash at home
OptionD: Exemption from filing Bill of Entry on imports
Explanation: Paragraph 1.26 of FTP 2023 grants Status Holders the privilege of self-certification of origin, 100% exemption from furnishing Bank Guarantees under duty exemption schemes, priority customs clearance, and preferential treatment. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 1.26)
CorrectText: Authorization to self-certify Certificate of Origin (non-preferential) and exemption from furnishing Bank Guarantee under FTP duty exemption schemes
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Privileges of Status Holders

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: What is the purpose of the RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products) Scheme under Chapter 4 of FTP 2023?
OptionA: To refund Basic Customs Duty paid on capital goods
OptionB: To provide a direct export subsidy illegal under WTO rules
OptionC: To provide zero-interest export credit loans
OptionD: To remit embedded central, state, and local duties/taxes (such as electricity duty, VAT on fuel, stamp duty) not refunded under any other mechanism, via electronic transferable scrips on ICEGATE
Explanation: Paragraph 4.54 of FTP 2023 outlines RoDTEP as a WTO-compliant mechanism to rebate unrefunded central, state, and local levies embedded in exported products, issued as electronic transferable duty credit scrips in the ICEGATE ledger. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 4.54)
CorrectText: To remit embedded central, state, and local duties/taxes (such as electricity duty, VAT on fuel, stamp duty) not refunded under any other mechanism, via electronic transferable scrips on ICEGATE
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — RoDTEP Scheme

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: What does "SCOMET" stand for under the Foreign Trade Policy and Indian trade regulations?
OptionA: Standard Commodity Organization for Maritime and Electronic Trade
OptionB: Strategic Committee on Monetary and Exchange Transactions
OptionC: Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies (dual-use items regulated for international security)
OptionD: Standard Customs Operations for Marine Export Transport
Explanation: SCOMET stands for Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies. Found in Appendix 3 of Schedule 2 of ITC(HS), these items are dual-use goods whose export is strictly controlled or prohibited. (Source: Chapter 10 FTP 2023 / DGFT)
CorrectText: Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies (dual-use items regulated for international security)
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — SCOMET Regulations

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under the Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration and Paperless Processing) Regulations, 2018, which form and color designation correspond to a Bill of Entry for Home Consumption?
OptionA: Form II — Yellow Bill of Entry
OptionB: Form IV — Blue Bill of Entry
OptionC: Form I — White Bill of Entry
OptionD: Form III — Green Bill of Entry
Explanation: Under the regulations and customs procedure: Form I is for Home Consumption (White), Form II is for Warehousing/Into-Bond (Yellow), and Form III is for Ex-Bond clearance for home consumption (Green). (Source: Bill of Entry Regulations 2018 / R.K. Jain)
CorrectText: Form I — White Bill of Entry
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Forms of Bill of Entry

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962, an Advance or Prior Bill of Entry may be filed up to how many days prior to the expected arrival of the vessel or aircraft?
Explanation: Section 46(3) permits presentation of a Bill of Entry at any time not exceeding 30 days prior to the expected arrival of the vessel or aircraft by which the goods have been shipped for importation into India. (Source: Section 46(3) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 30 days
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Advance / Prior Filing

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: In customs manual/EDI documentation practices, what color corresponds to a Duty Drawback Shipping Bill?
Explanation: Customs EDI / shipping documentation standards designate: White for Free Shipping Bill, Green for Duty Drawback Shipping Bill, Yellow for Dutiable Shipping Bill, and Blue for Export Promotion Schemes (Advance Authorisation / EPCG / EOU). (Source: CBIC Customs Manual)
CorrectText: Green Shipping Bill
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Color Categorisation of Shipping Bills

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: What is the operational consequence when an electronic Bill of Entry is facilitated under the Risk Management System (RMS) Green Channel?
OptionA: The goods must be examined 100% by the Docks Appraiser
OptionB: The Bill of Entry is cleared without physical examination and without concurrent assessment by the Appraising Group, moving directly to duty payment and Out of Charge
OptionC: The importer is exempt from paying IGST
OptionD: The Bill of Entry must be reviewed by the Commissioner in person
Explanation: RMS facilitation (Green Channel) allows low-risk consignments to be processed without physical examination or assessment by the Appraising Group, enabling direct duty payment and delivery (Direct Port Delivery / DPD). (Source: CBIC RMS Guidelines / Circular 43/2005)
CorrectText: The Bill of Entry is cleared without physical examination and without concurrent assessment by the Appraising Group, moving directly to duty payment and Out of Charge
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Green Channel Clearance

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: What is the fundamental procedural difference between "First Check" and "Second Check" examination of imported goods?
OptionA: First check is optional; second check is governed by the police
OptionB: First check is done by the Customs Broker; second check is done by the importer
OptionC: First check entails examination and sampling of goods before assessment of duty; second check entails assessment of duty first, followed by examination at the docks before Out of Charge
OptionD: First check applies only to air cargo; second check applies to sea cargo
Explanation: Under First Check (requested by importer when parameters/description are unknown), examination occurs before assessment. Under Second Check (the standard default procedure), assessment occurs first, and examination is carried out in the shed/docks before granting Out of Charge. (Source: CBIC Customs Manual / R.K. Jain)
CorrectText: First check entails examination and sampling of goods before assessment of duty; second check entails assessment of duty first, followed by examination at the docks before Out of Charge
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — First Check vs Second Check

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: Under the CBIC "Turant Customs" initiative, how does Faceless Assessment operate?
OptionA: Customs officers inspect cargo wearing biometric visors
OptionB: Assessments are outsourced to private third-party auditing firms
OptionC: All imported goods are examined exclusively at the importer's residence
OptionD: Bills of Entry are assigned anonymously by an automated algorithm to virtual Faceless Assessment Groups (FAGs) across the country, delinked from the physical port of import
Explanation: Turant Customs introduced Faceless Assessment, whereby Bills of Entry are electronically and randomly routed to virtual Faceless Assessment Groups (FAGs) stationed anywhere in India, eliminating physical interface between trade and assessing officers. (Source: CBIC Circular No. 27/2020-Customs)
CorrectText: Bills of Entry are assigned anonymously by an automated algorithm to virtual Faceless Assessment Groups (FAGs) across the country, delinked from the physical port of import
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Faceless Assessment Groups (FAGs)

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: What is "e-Sanchit" on ICEGATE, and what identifier is generated upon uploading supporting documents?
OptionA: A portal for tracking vessel speed
OptionB: An online paperless repository for uploading digitally signed PDF supporting documents, which generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN) linked to the declaration
OptionC: A portal for booking truck appointments at ICDs
OptionD: An automated payment gateway for paying shipping line detention charges
Explanation: e-Sanchit (electronic Storage and Access of Digitally Signed Supporting Documents) allows paperless filing on ICEGATE. Each uploaded supporting document (invoice, packing list, certificate) generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN). (Source: CBIC Circular No. 40/2017-Customs)
CorrectText: An online paperless repository for uploading digitally signed PDF supporting documents, which generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN) linked to the declaration
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Image Reference Number (IRN)

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: Under Section 51A of the Customs Act, 1962, how do importers and Customs Brokers make electronic payments of duty, interest, and penalties on ICEGATE?
OptionA: Through the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL) maintained on the customs automated system
OptionB: By sending an account-payee demand draft to CBIC headquarters
OptionC: By depositing physical cash at the customs cash counter only
OptionD: By offsetting export incentives directly without ledger entry
Explanation: Section 51A mandates the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL) on ICEGATE, wherein funds are deposited via net banking/NEFT/RTGS and then utilized to debit and pay customs duties, interest, and penalties electronically. (Source: Section 51A Customs Act, 1962 / Customs ECL Regs 2022)
CorrectText: Through the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL) maintained on the customs automated system
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 74 of the Customs Act, 1962, what percentage of import duty is granted as drawback when imported duty-paid goods are re-exported as such without being put to any use in India?
Explanation: Section 74(1) provides that where imported goods are re-exported without being used, 98% of the import duty paid at the time of importation shall be repaid as drawback. (Source: Section 74(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 98% of the import duty paid
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Re-Export of Unused Goods

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Notification No. 19/65-Customs as amended, when imported goods are used before re-export under Section 74, what is the maximum period of use beyond which NO drawback is permissible?
Explanation: Under Notification No. 19/65-Cus as amended, drawback on goods used before re-export is reduced on a sliding scale for each quarter of use, and where the period of use exceeds 18 months, the allowable drawback is NIL. (Source: Notification No. 19/65-Customs as amended)
CorrectText: 18 months
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Notification No. 19/65-Customs (Used Goods)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 74 of the Customs Act, 1962, imported goods must be entered for export within what time period from the date of payment of duty on importation?
OptionA: 5 years, with permission of the Port Trust
OptionD: 2 years, extendable by the Board (CBIC) on sufficient cause shown
Explanation: Section 74(1) mandates that the goods must be entered for export within 2 years from the date of payment of duty on the importation thereof, subject to extension by CBIC on sufficient cause shown. (Source: Section 74(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 2 years, extendable by the Board (CBIC) on sufficient cause shown
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Statutory Time Limit for Section 74

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Section: All Industry Rates vs Brand Rate
Question: Under Rule 6 and Rule 7 of the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017, when may an exporter apply for fixation of a Brand Rate or Special Brand Rate of duty drawback?
OptionA: Only when export goods are manufactured in an SEZ
OptionB: Whenever the exporter prefers cash payment over scrips
OptionC: Where the export product has no All Industry Rate (AIR), or where the AIR covers less than four-fifths (80%) of the actual duties paid on inputs
OptionD: Only for goods exported to SAARC countries
Explanation: Under Rules 6 and 7 of the Drawback Rules 2017, Brand Rate is fixed when an item does not figure in the AIR schedule, or where the exporter demonstrates that the notified AIR drawback covers less than 80% (four-fifths) of the duties actually paid on imported/domestic inputs. (Source: Drawback Rules 2017 / CBIC)
CorrectText: Where the export product has no All Industry Rate (AIR), or where the AIR covers less than four-fifths (80%) of the actual duties paid on inputs
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — All Industry Rates vs Brand Rate

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 76 of the Customs Act, 1962, duty drawback shall NOT be allowed in which of the following circumstances?
OptionA: If the market price of the export goods is less than the amount of drawback claimed, or if the claim is less than Rs 50
OptionB: If goods are exported by air
OptionC: If the export invoice is denominated in Euros
OptionD: If the exporter is a merchant exporter rather than a manufacturer
Explanation: Section 76(1) bars drawback in respect of any goods the market price of which is less than the amount of drawback due thereon, and Section 76(2) provides that no drawback shall be paid where the claim is less than Rs 50. (Source: Section 76 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: If the market price of the export goods is less than the amount of drawback claimed, or if the claim is less than Rs 50
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Prohibition of Drawback

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Rule 96 of the CGST Rules, 2017, how is the refund of IGST paid on export of goods processed?
OptionA: Refund is allowed only if no GST return is ever revised
OptionB: The exporter must submit a physical manual claim to the jurisdictional GST Range Officer within 15 days
OptionC: Refund is issued as physical promissory notes by the Reserve Bank of India
OptionD: The Shipping Bill filed by the exporter is itself deemed to be an application for refund once the Departure Manifest/EGM and GSTR-3B/GSTR-1 are filed, processed automatically via ICEGATE
Explanation: Rule 96 provides that the Shipping Bill having an IGST payment declaration is deemed to be a refund application. ICEGATE automatically validates the data with GSTN (Table 6A of GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B) and credits the refund directly via PFMS. (Source: Rule 96 CGST Rules / CBIC Circular 43/2017-Cus)
CorrectText: The Shipping Bill filed by the exporter is itself deemed to be an application for refund once the Departure Manifest/EGM and GSTR-3B/GSTR-1 are filed, processed automatically via ICEGATE
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Rule 96 of CGST Rules, 2017

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: In the automated processing of IGST refunds on export of goods on ICEGATE, what does the frequent error code "SB005" signify?
OptionB: Exporter's bank account is in an unapproved overseas bank
OptionC: Invoice number, date, and port code mismatch between the Shipping Bill data on ICEGATE and Table 6A of GSTR-1 on the GST portal
OptionD: Failure to obtain FSSAI license for engineering goods
Explanation: Error SB005 represents an invoice mismatch: the invoice number, date, or port code declared in the Shipping Bill does not match the details uploaded in Table 6A of GSTR-1, preventing automated clearance of IGST refund. (Source: CBIC Advisory on IGST Refund / ICEGATE)
CorrectText: Invoice number, date, and port code mismatch between the Shipping Bill data on ICEGATE and Table 6A of GSTR-1 on the GST portal
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — ICEGATE Error Code SB005

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: What is the crucial statutory difference between Section 13 (Pilferage) and Section 23 (Lost or Destroyed Goods) of the Customs Act, 1962?
OptionA: Section 13 requires prior FIR registration; Section 23 requires a certificate from the President of India
OptionB: Section 13 applies only to exports; Section 23 applies only to imports
OptionC: Under Section 13, duty is not payable if goods are pilfered before clearance/warehousing order; under Section 23, duty is remitted on goods lost (other than pilferage) or destroyed before clearance for home consumption
OptionD: Section 13 applies to warehoused goods; Section 23 does not
Explanation: Under Section 13, the importer is automatically not liable to pay duty if goods are pilfered before clearance for home consumption or warehousing (and custodian pays under Sec 45(3)). Section 23 covers non-pilferage losses and destruction (e.g. fire, acts of God) at any time before home consumption clearance. (Source: Section 13 & 23 Customs Act, 1962 / R.K. Jain)
CorrectText: Under Section 13, duty is not payable if goods are pilfered before clearance/warehousing order; under Section 23, duty is remitted on goods lost (other than pilferage) or destroyed before clearance for home consumption
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 13 vs Section 23

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 3 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what is the General Free Allowance (GFA) for an Indian resident or tourist of Indian origin arriving by air from any country other than Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar?
Explanation: Under Rule 3, an Indian resident or foreigner residing in India or a tourist of Indian origin arriving from countries other than Nepal, Bhutan or Myanmar is allowed clearance free of duty for articles up to an aggregate value of Rs 50,000 (excluding Annexure I goods). Foreign tourists get Rs 15,000. (Source: Rule 3 Baggage Rules, 2016)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3 — General Free Allowance (GFA)

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Section: Rule 4 — Arriving from Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar
Question: Under Rule 4 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what is the General Free Allowance for a passenger arriving from Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar across land borders versus arriving by air?
Explanation: Under Rule 4, passengers arriving from Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar by land borders have a GFA of Nil (only used personal effects are free). If arriving by air, the GFA is Rs 15,000. (Source: Rule 4 Baggage Rules, 2016)
CorrectText: Land: Nil; Air: Rs 15,000
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Rule 4 — Arriving from Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Rule 6 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what are the weight and value limitations for duty-free clearance of gold jewelry brought by an Indian passenger who has resided abroad for more than one year?
OptionB: Gentlemen: Up to 20 grams with value cap of Rs 50,000; Ladies: Up to 40 grams with value cap of Rs 1,00,000
OptionC: Gold jewelry is completely exempt with zero weight limit
Explanation: Rule 6 provides that a passenger residing abroad for over one year may bring duty-free jewelry in bona fide baggage: gentleman passenger up to 20 grams (value ceiling Rs 50,000); lady passenger up to 40 grams (value ceiling Rs 1,00,000). (Source: Rule 6 Baggage Rules, 2016)
CorrectText: Gentlemen: Up to 20 grams with value cap of Rs 50,000; Ladies: Up to 40 grams with value cap of Rs 1,00,000
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Rule 6 — Jewelry Allowance

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Which of the following items is included in Annexure I of the Baggage Rules, 2016 (and is therefore strictly EXCLUDED from the General Free Allowance and always dutiable)?
Explanation: Annexure I includes: Firearms, cartridges > 50, cigarettes > 100, cigars > 25, tobacco > 125g, alcohol/wine > 2 litres, gold/silver other than ornaments, and Flat Panel (LCD/LED/Plasma) TVs. These can never be cleared under the GFA. (Source: Annexure I Baggage Rules, 2016)
CorrectText: Flat panel (LCD / LED / Plasma) Television
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Annexure I — Excluded Articles

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: What is the standard effective rate of customs duty charged on dutiable passenger baggage under Heading 9803 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975?
OptionA: Flat 50% ad valorem with zero cesses
OptionC: 35% Basic Customs Duty + 10% Social Welfare Surcharge (effective 38.5%)
Explanation: Baggage under Heading 9803 attracts a statutory BCD rate of 35%, along with a 10% Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) on duty, resulting in an effective customs duty rate of 38.5%. (Source: Customs Tariff Heading 9803 / Notification 26/2016-Cus)
CorrectText: 35% Basic Customs Duty + 10% Social Welfare Surcharge (effective 38.5%)
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Duty Rate on Dutiable Baggage

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Section 20 of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the default legal principle regarding goods produced or manufactured in India that are exported and subsequently re-imported?
OptionA: They can enter only under a Special Economic Zone permit
OptionB: They can only be imported via parcel post
OptionC: They are permanently exempt from all taxes because they originated in India
OptionD: They are liable to customs duty and subject to conditions/restrictions as if they were imported for the first time, unless exempted by notification
Explanation: Section 20 states that goods produced/manufactured in India, when re-imported, shall be liable to customs duty and subject to conditions as if imported for the first time, save as otherwise provided by Central Government exemption notifications (e.g. Notif 45/2017-Cus). (Source: Section 20 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: They are liable to customs duty and subject to conditions/restrictions as if they were imported for the first time, unless exempted by notification
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Re-Importation of Indian Goods

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Notification No. 45/2017-Customs, when Indian goods are exported for repair or alteration abroad and re-imported within 3 years, what is the customs duty liability on re-import?
OptionA: Completely free of all duties and GST without assessment
OptionB: Customs duty is payable only on the fair cost of repairs/alterations, cost of materials added, and two-way international freight and insurance
OptionC: Full customs duty on the entire value of the machinery as if newly purchased
Explanation: Under Notification No. 45/2017-Customs, goods exported for repairs/alterations and re-imported within 3 years pay customs duty only on the value of repairs, materials added, and freight + insurance both ways, provided the goods are identified as the same. (Source: Notification No. 45/2017-Customs / CBIC)
CorrectText: Customs duty is payable only on the fair cost of repairs/alterations, cost of materials added, and two-way international freight and insurance
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Re-Import After Repairs Abroad

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Section: Re-Import of Goods Exported Under Drawback / IGST Refund
Question: When goods exported under claim of duty drawback or IGST refund are re-imported into India within 3 years (e.g. due to rejection by foreign buyer), what is the condition for clearance under Notification No. 45/2017-Customs?
OptionA: The goods can only be released after 1 year in a bonded warehouse
OptionB: The importer must repay the amount of duty drawback or IGST refund availed at the time of export
OptionC: The importer must surrender his IEC to DGFT
OptionD: The goods must be auctioned by the custodian
Explanation: Notification No. 45/2017-Customs provides that when exported goods are returned due to rejection or lack of demand within 3 years, they are exempt from basic customs duty subject to repayment of the drawback availed or refund of IGST claimed at export. (Source: Notification No. 45/2017-Customs / CBIC Circular)
CorrectText: The importer must repay the amount of duty drawback or IGST refund availed at the time of export
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Re-Import of Goods Exported Under Drawback / IGST Refund

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods & Services) Regulations, 2015, what is the statutory time period within which the full export value of goods must be realized and repatriated to India?
OptionA: 90 days from the date of Shipping Bill
OptionB: 3 years from the date of realization of the bill of lading
OptionC: 9 months from the date of export (15 months if goods are exported to an overseas warehouse established with RBI approval)
OptionD: 180 days from the date of the commercial invoice
Explanation: Under Regulation 9 of the FEMA (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations 2015 as amended by RBI, the realization period is 9 months from the date of export (15 months in case of goods exported to an approved warehouse abroad). (Source: RBI Master Direction on Export of Goods / FEMA 1999)
CorrectText: 9 months from the date of export (15 months if goods are exported to an overseas warehouse established with RBI approval)
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Export Realisation & Repatriation Period

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: What are "EDPMS" and "IDPMS" deployed by the Reserve Bank of India in coordination with Customs?
OptionA: Private software for calculating freight forwarding commissions
OptionB: Maritime security tracking systems operated by the Indian Navy
OptionC: Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS) and Import Data Processing and Monitoring System (IDPMS) for tracking export realization and import outward remittances against Customs declarations
OptionD: Electronic systems for inspecting container seals
Explanation: EDPMS and IDPMS are RBI IT platforms integrating Customs Shipping Bills and Bills of Entry with Authorized Dealer banks to monitor real-time realization of export proceeds (e-BRC) and settlement of import remittances. (Source: RBI Master Directions / ICEGATE)
CorrectText: Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS) and Import Data Processing and Monitoring System (IDPMS) for tracking export realization and import outward remittances against Customs declarations
