Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — EDPMS and IDPMS Systems

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under FEMA regulations, an arriving passenger entering India must submit a Currency Declaration Form (CDF) to Customs when bringing in foreign currency notes exceeding which thresholds?
OptionA: When aggregate value of foreign currency notes exceeds USD 5,000 or aggregate value of currency notes plus travellers cheques exceeds USD 10,000
OptionD: Declaration is optional irrespective of amount
Explanation: Under FEMA (Manner of Receipt and Payment) Regulations, a passenger must declare foreign exchange on a CDF if foreign currency bank notes exceed USD 5,000 or total foreign currency (notes + travellers cheques) exceeds USD 10,000 (or equivalent). (Source: RBI Master Direction / Customs Baggage Guide)
CorrectText: When aggregate value of foreign currency notes exceeds USD 5,000 or aggregate value of currency notes plus travellers cheques exceeds USD 10,000
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Foreign Currency Declaration (CDF)

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under RBI FEMA regulations, what is the maximum amount of Indian currency notes that an Indian resident may carry when travelling outside India (other than to Nepal or Bhutan)?
Explanation: Under Regulation 8 of FEMA (Export and Import of Currency) Regulations, an Indian resident travelling abroad (other than Nepal and Bhutan) may carry Indian currency notes up to a maximum of Rs 25,000 per person. (Source: RBI Notification No. FEMA 6(R)/RB-2015)
CorrectText: Rs 25,000 per person
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Carriage of Indian Currency Notes

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under Rule 6 of the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, which of the following declarations is MANDATORY on all imported pre-packaged commodities sold in India?
OptionA: Name and address of manufacturer and importer, generic name, net quantity, month/year of manufacture/import, MRP (inclusive of all taxes in INR), and consumer care details
OptionB: Only the country of origin in French or English
OptionD: Only the barcode and foreign factory address
Explanation: Rule 6 of Legal Metrology (PC) Rules mandates: (1) Name & address of manufacturer/importer, (2) Common/generic name, (3) Net quantity, (4) Month & year of mfg/import, (5) Maximum Retail Price (MRP inclusive of all taxes), and (6) Consumer care details. (Source: Legal Metrology (PC) Rules, 2011 / Ministry of Consumer Affairs)
CorrectText: Name and address of manufacturer and importer, generic name, net quantity, month/year of manufacture/import, MRP (inclusive of all taxes in INR), and consumer care details
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 6 — Mandatory Declarations

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: If imported pre-packaged goods arrive without the mandatory Legal Metrology declarations, what customs relief is available under DGFT Notification No. 44/2000-Customs?
OptionA: The importer is issued a non-bailable arrest warrant
OptionB: Goods are allowed for home consumption if the broker gives a verbal undertaking
OptionC: The goods may be deposited in a customs bonded warehouse under Section 49 / Section 58, and mandatory labels affixed prior to clearance for home consumption
OptionD: The cargo must be destroyed immediately without notice
Explanation: Under DGFT Notification No. 44/2000-Cus read with CBIC Circulars, imported pre-packaged goods can be moved into a bonded warehouse where labeling/stickering of MRP and mandatory declarations can be completed prior to clearance for home consumption. (Source: DGFT Notif 44/2000-Cus / CBIC Circular No. 19/2011-Cus)
CorrectText: The goods may be deposited in a customs bonded warehouse under Section 49 / Section 58, and mandatory labels affixed prior to clearance for home consumption
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Labeling in Bonded Warehouses

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under the Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017, what is the mandatory minimum remaining shelf life of imported food products at the time of customs clearance?
OptionB: Not less than 60% of the total original shelf life of the product at the time of import clearance
OptionC: At least 90 days regardless of total shelf life
OptionD: At least 25% of total shelf life
Explanation: Regulation 5(6) of FSSAI (Import) Regulations, 2017 provides that Customs shall not clear any imported food item unless it has a valid shelf life of not less than 60% of its original total shelf life at the time of import. (Source: FSSAI (Import) Regulations, 2017 / CBIC SWIFT)
CorrectText: Not less than 60% of the total original shelf life of the product at the time of import clearance
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Shelf Life Requirement at Import

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: How is food safety import clearance obtained for food consignments entering India through Customs?
OptionA: Food items do not require any FSSAI clearance if imported by air
OptionB: By obtaining clearance from local municipal food inspectors at the dock
OptionC: Through the ICEGATE SWIFT (Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade) portal, where FSSAI Authorised Officer conducts document verification, visual inspection, laboratory testing, and issues an online No Objection Certificate (NOC)
OptionD: By visiting FSSAI headquarters in New Delhi with a sample
Explanation: Under the Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade (SWIFT) on ICEGATE, food import entries are automatically routed to the FSSAI Food Import Clearance System (FICS). An Authorised Officer (AO) samples, tests, and issues an electronic NOC or Non-Conformance Certificate (NCC). (Source: FSSAI Import Regulations 2017 / CBIC SWIFT Guidelines)
CorrectText: Through the ICEGATE SWIFT (Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade) portal, where FSSAI Authorised Officer conducts document verification, visual inspection, laboratory testing, and issues an online No Objection Certificate (NOC)
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Import Clearance & SWIFT Interface

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 5 of CBLR, 2018, what is the minimum educational qualification generally prescribed for an individual applicant to appear for the Regulation 6 examination?
OptionA: Postgraduate degree in Maritime Law exclusively
Explanation: Regulation 5(1) prescribes graduation from a recognised university as a fundamental educational qualification for an applicant appearing for the examination under Regulation 6. (Source: Regulation 5 CBLR, 2018)
CorrectText: Graduate from a recognised university
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 5

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 10(n) of CBLR, 2018, how must a Customs Broker verify the correctness of the Importer Exporter Code (IEC), GSTIN, identity, and address of the client?
OptionA: Only through a police verification certificate
OptionB: Only through a self-declaration letter signed by the client
OptionC: Any one document chosen at the broker's discretion
OptionD: Using reliable, independent, authentic documents, data or information, not being documents furnished by the client himself
Explanation: Regulation 10(n) mandates that the Customs Broker must verify the identity and address of the client using reliable, independent, authentic documents, data or information, not merely documents furnished by the client himself. (Source: Regulation 10(n) CBLR, 2018 / KYC Guidelines)
CorrectText: Using reliable, independent, authentic documents, data or information, not being documents furnished by the client himself
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 17(5) of CBLR, 2018, within what time period must the Inquiry Officer appointed by the Commissioner submit his inquiry report?
OptionA: 30 days from the date of appointment
OptionB: 90 days from the date of issue of the notice
OptionD: 180 days from the date of alleged contravention
Explanation: Regulation 17(5) mandates that the Inquiry Officer must complete the inquiry and submit his report within 90 days from the date of issue of the notice under Regulation 17(1). (Source: Regulation 17(5) CBLR, 2018)
CorrectText: 90 days from the date of issue of the notice
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 17

Chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
Question: Under the three-tier AEO Programme for importers and exporters notified by CBIC, which tier is granted solely on the basis of desktop verification without physical on-site verification?
Explanation: Under Circular No. 33/2016-Customs, AEO-T1 status is granted solely based on desktop verification of documentary compliance and clean fiscal history; physical site verification is not required. (Source: CBIC Circular 33/2016-Cus / AEO Guidelines)
CorrectText: AEO-T1
Topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Circular No. 33/2016-Customs

Chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
Section: AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 Bank Guarantee Benefits
Question: What is the percentage waiver on furnishing Bank Guarantees granted to an entity holding AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 status under customs duty exemption and facilitation schemes?
Explanation: Under the AEO Programme, AEO-T2 holders are granted a 50% waiver on bank guarantee requirements, while AEO-T3 holders enjoy a 100% waiver of bank guarantee under all duty exemption and remission schemes. (Source: Circular 33/2016-Customs)
Topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 Bank Guarantee Benefits

Chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
Question: Which of the following supply chain actors is eligible to apply for AEO-LO (Logistics Operator) certification?
OptionA: Customs Brokers, Logistics Providers, Custodians / Terminal Operators, and Warehouse Operators
OptionB: Only software consultants developing EDI formats
OptionC: Foreign manufacturers having no presence in India
Explanation: AEO-LO is specifically designed for intermediate supply chain entities including Customs Brokers, Logistics Providers, Custodians or Terminal Operators, and Warehouse Operators. (Source: CBIC Circular No. 33/2016-Customs)
CorrectText: Customs Brokers, Logistics Providers, Custodians / Terminal Operators, and Warehouse Operators
Topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — AEO-LO Eligibility

Chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
Question: What is the statutory certificate validity period for AEO-T1, AEO-T2, and AEO-T3 holders respectively under the Indian AEO Programme?
OptionA: AEO-T1: 1 year; AEO-T2: 2 years; AEO-T3: 3 years
OptionB: AEO-T1: 3 years; AEO-T2: 3 years; AEO-T3: 5 years
OptionC: AEO-T1: 5 years; AEO-T2: 5 years; AEO-T3: Permanent
OptionD: All tiers are valid for 10 years
Explanation: Under CBIC AEO guidelines, AEO-T1 and AEO-T2 certifications are valid for 3 years, while AEO-T3 and AEO-LO certifications are valid for 5 years, subject to continuous compliance. (Source: CBIC Circular 33/2016-Cus)
CorrectText: AEO-T1: 3 years; AEO-T2: 3 years; AEO-T3: 5 years
Topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Validity of AEO Certificates

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Section 28DA of the Customs Act, 1962 read with CAROTAR, 2020, what is the primary legal responsibility placed on an importer claiming preferential tariff treatment under a Free Trade Agreement (FTA)?
OptionA: The importer must exercise origin due diligence, possess sufficient information to satisfy origin criteria (Form I), and cannot rely blindly on the Certificate of Origin
OptionB: The importer must obtain written consent from the State Government
OptionC: The importer has zero responsibility once a Certificate of Origin (COO) is issued
OptionD: The importer must pay a mandatory origin verification tax of 5%
Explanation: Section 28DA and Rule 3 of CAROTAR 2020 mandate that an importer claiming preferential tariff must exercise due diligence, possess origin-related information as outlined in Form I, and be satisfied that the goods meet origin criteria. (Source: Section 28DA Customs Act / CAROTAR 2020)
CorrectText: The importer must exercise origin due diligence, possess sufficient information to satisfy origin criteria (Form I), and cannot rely blindly on the Certificate of Origin
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Section 28DA / Rule 3

Chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
Section: Rule 5 - Time Limit to Furnish Information
Question: Under Rule 5(1) of CAROTAR, 2020, when the proper officer raises a requisition for origin-related information or documents, within what time period must the importer furnish the required details?
Explanation: Rule 5(1) of CAROTAR 2020 requires the importer to provide the requisitioned origin information and supporting documents within 10 working days from the date of receipt of the requisition from the proper officer. (Source: Rule 5 CAROTAR 2020)
CorrectText: 10 working days
Topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Rule 5 - Time Limit to Furnish Information

Chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
Question: Under Rule 6 of CAROTAR, 2020, who conducts retroactive verification of origin with the Issuing Authority of the exporting country?
OptionA: The private shipping line carrying the goods
OptionB: Any Appraiser on duty at the dock
OptionC: The Indian High Commission directly without customs involvement
OptionD: The designated Nodal Officer through the CBIC FTA Cell
Explanation: Rule 6 specifies that verification requests to the verification authority of the exporting country shall be sent by the designated Nodal Officer through the CBIC Trade / FTA Cell. (Source: Rule 6 CAROTAR 2020 / CBIC Circular 38/2020-Cus)
CorrectText: The designated Nodal Officer through the CBIC FTA Cell
Topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Rule 6 - Verification from Exporting Country

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Rule 4 of the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022, what identifier is generated on the Common Portal upon submitting prior one-time intimation?
Explanation: Rule 4 of IGCR Rules 2022 provides that upon submitting one-time prior information on the common portal (ICEGATE), an IGCR Identification Number (IIN) is automatically generated. (Source: Rule 4 IGCR Rules, 2022)
CorrectText: IGCR Identification Number (IIN)
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 4 - One-Time Intimation & IIN

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Rule 6 of the IGCR Rules, 2022, by which day of the succeeding month must the importer submit an electronic monthly statement on the Common Portal detailing the receipt and consumption of concessional duty goods?
Explanation: Rule 6 of IGCR Rules 2022 requires the importer to submit a monthly statement on the common portal by the tenth day of the following month, accounting for all goods received and consumed. (Source: Rule 6 IGCR Rules, 2022)
CorrectText: 10th of the month
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 6 - Monthly Statement

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Section: Rule 7 & 8 - Job Work of Concessional Goods
Question: Under the IGCR Rules, 2022, what is the maximum time limit within which goods sent for job work from the importer's manufacturing premises must be received back?
OptionC: 6 months from the date of sending the goods (extendable by the jurisdictional officer)
Explanation: Rule 7(3) of IGCR Rules 2022 mandates that goods sent for job work shall be received back within a period of six months from the date of dispatch, subject to extension by the jurisdictional officer. (Source: Rule 7 IGCR Rules, 2022)
CorrectText: 6 months from the date of sending the goods (extendable by the jurisdictional officer)
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 7 & 8 - Job Work of Concessional Goods

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 28H of the Customs Act, 1962, on which of the following questions can an eligible applicant seek an Advance Ruling from the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings (CAAR)?
OptionB: Only on the personal income tax slab of the importer
OptionC: Classification of goods, applicability of exemption notifications, and principles of valuation under Section 14
OptionD: On whether the customs duty can be waived completely on political grounds
Explanation: Section 28H(2) permits advance rulings on: (a) classification of goods, (b) applicability of exemption notifications, (c) valuation principles under Section 14, and (d) origin determination under trade agreements. (Source: Section 28H Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Classification of goods, applicability of exemption notifications, and principles of valuation under Section 14
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 28H

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 28-I(6) of the Customs Act, 1962, the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings (CAAR) is required to pronounce its advance ruling within what time limit from the date of receipt of the application?
Explanation: Section 28-I(6) provides that the Authority shall pronounce its advance ruling in writing within three months from the date of receipt of the application. (Source: Section 28-I(6) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 3 months
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 28-I

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 28J of the Customs Act, 1962, an advance ruling pronounced by CAAR is binding on:
OptionB: All foreign shipping lines operating in Indian waters
OptionC: All importers across India indiscriminately as a general law
OptionD: Only the applicant who sought it and in respect of the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs and his subordinate officers
Explanation: Section 28J(1) specifies that an advance ruling shall be binding only on the applicant who sought it and on the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs in respect of the concerned transaction. (Source: Section 28J Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Only the applicant who sought it and in respect of the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs and his subordinate officers
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 28J

Chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
Question: Under Section 99A of the Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, what are the two statutory forms of customs audit conducted by the department?
OptionA: Police Investigation Audit and Municipal Audit
OptionB: RBI Currency Audit and DGFT Quota Audit
OptionC: Pre-shipment Audit and Port Trust Audit
OptionD: Transaction Based Audit (TBA) and Premises Based Audit (PBA)
Explanation: Section 99A read with Customs Audit Regulations 2018 recognizes Transaction Based Audit (TBA) at customs stations and Premises Based Audit (PBA) conducted at the registered commercial premises of the auditee. (Source: Section 99A Customs Act / Customs Audit Regs 2018)
CorrectText: Transaction Based Audit (TBA) and Premises Based Audit (PBA)
Topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Section 99A / Customs Audit Regulations, 2018

Chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
Question: Under Regulation 4 of the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, for what minimum period must an auditee preserve all customs declarations, invoices, and accounting records relevant to imported/export goods?
OptionA: 5 years from the date of clearance of goods
Explanation: Regulation 4 requires every auditee to maintain and preserve books of accounts, records, documents and customs declarations for a period of not less than 5 years from the date of clearance of the goods. (Source: Regulation 4 Customs Audit Regulations, 2018)
CorrectText: 5 years from the date of clearance of goods
Topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Regulation 4 - Preservation of Records

Chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
Question: Under the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, what advance intimation notice must ordinarily be served on an auditee prior to conducting a Premises Based Audit (PBA)?
OptionA: No notice is required; surprise visits are mandatory
OptionC: At least 15 days advance notice in writing
Explanation: Regulation 5 mandates that the proper officer shall give an advance notice in writing of at least 15 days to the auditee before conducting an audit at their premises. (Source: Regulation 5 Customs Audit Regulations, 2018)
CorrectText: At least 15 days advance notice in writing
Topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Notice for Premises Based Audit

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 (HCCAR), what is the statutory status of an entity appointed to handle and store imported goods in a customs area?
OptionA: Customs Cargo Services Provider (CCSP) / Custodian under Section 45
OptionD: Sole Agent of the Ministry of Commerce
Explanation: Under HCCAR 2009, persons handling imported or export goods in customs areas are designated as Customs Cargo Services Providers (CCSPs) and operate as Custodians under Section 45 of the Customs Act. (Source: HCCAR 2009 / Section 45)
CorrectText: Customs Cargo Services Provider (CCSP) / Custodian under Section 45
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 5 & Section 45

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Regulation 5(1)(h) of HCCAR, 2009, a Customs Cargo Services Provider (CCSP) must install high-definition CCTV systems and preserve the recorded video footage for a minimum period of:
Explanation: Regulation 5(1)(h) of HCCAR 2009 mandates that CCSPs must maintain 24x7 CCTV coverage of all cargo handling, entry, and exit points and preserve the video recordings for a minimum of 30 days for inspection by customs. (Source: Regulation 5(1)(h) HCCAR 2009)
CorrectText: 30 days
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — CCTV Video Footage Retention

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under the revised SVB guidelines issued vide CBIC Circular No. 05/2016-Customs, which transactions are investigated by the Special Valuation Branch?
OptionA: All imports exceeding Rs 10 Crores in value
OptionB: Imports between related persons under Rule 2(2) of CVR 2007 where relationship may have influenced price, and cases involving royalties, license fees or subsequent resale proceeds
OptionC: All shipments arriving from neighboring land border countries
OptionD: Only imports of gold bullion by scheduled banks
Explanation: Circular No. 05/2016-Customs provides that SVBs investigate cases where buyer and seller are related under Rule 2(2) of CVR 2007 and there is prima facie ground to believe the relationship influenced invoice price, or where royalty/license fees/assists are involved. (Source: Circular 05/2016-Customs)
CorrectText: Imports between related persons under Rule 2(2) of CVR 2007 where relationship may have influenced price, and cases involving royalties, license fees or subsequent resale proceeds
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Circular No. 05/2016-Customs

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: What is the general policy regarding Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) during the pendency of an SVB investigation under Circular No. 05/2016-Customs?
OptionA: EDD equal to 100% of the Basic Customs Duty
OptionB: Compulsory 10% cash deposit with the Reserve Bank of India
OptionC: Zero EDD is collected as a matter of standard practice; 1% EDD is levied only if the importer fails to submit the prescribed Annexure/information within 60 days
OptionD: Compulsory 5% EDD in every related party transaction
Explanation: Under the revamped SVB procedure, the practice of routinely imposing Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) was abolished. EDD @ 1% is imposed only if the importer fails to submit the completed questionnaire/documents within 60 days of requisition. (Source: CBIC Circular No. 05/2016-Customs)
CorrectText: Zero EDD is collected as a matter of standard practice; 1% EDD is levied only if the importer fails to submit the prescribed Annexure/information within 60 days
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) Policy

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Question: Under Heading 9801 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 read with Project Imports Regulations, 1986, what is the core commercial benefit of registering an industrial project under the Project Import scheme?
OptionA: Complete exemption from IGST without condition
OptionC: All project goods, machinery, and accompanying spare parts are assessed at a single uniform customs duty rate instead of separate itemized classifications under multiple tariff chapters
OptionD: Exemption from filing a Bill of Entry
Explanation: Project Imports scheme under Heading 9801 provides a single, uniform concessional rate of basic customs duty for all items, machinery, and initial spare parts imported for setting up a new plant or undertaking substantial expansion. (Source: Project Imports Regulations, 1986 / Chapter 98)
CorrectText: All project goods, machinery, and accompanying spare parts are assessed at a single uniform customs duty rate instead of separate itemized classifications under multiple tariff chapters
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Heading 9801 Scope

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Question: Under Regulation 7 of the Project Imports Regulations, 1986, within what time period after plant commissioning must the importer submit a plant completion certificate and reconciliation statement for finalization of contract?
Explanation: Regulation 7 requires the importer to submit a plant completion and commissioning certificate from a Chartered Engineer or sponsoring authority along with final reconciliation within three months (extendable up to six months by the Commissioner). (Source: Regulation 7 Project Imports Regulations, 1986)
CorrectText: 3 months (extendable up to 6 months)
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Plant Commissioning & Contract Finalization

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under the Courier Imports and Exports (Electronic Declaration and Processing) Regulations, 2010, which electronic declaration form is filed for commercial import cargo of high value?
Explanation: Under Courier Regulations 2010: CBE-XI is for documents, CBE-XII is for free gifts/samples up to Rs 10,000, CBE-XIII is for low value dutiable, CBE-XIV is for medium value, and CBE-XV is for commercial high-value goods. (Source: Courier Regulations, 2010 / CBIC)
CorrectText: Form CBE-XV
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Electronic Declaration Forms

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Which of the following commodities is completely prohibited from being imported or exported through courier mode under customs regulations?
OptionC: Precious stones, gold or silver in bullion, arms and ammunition, and live animals
Explanation: Regulation 2(2) strictly prohibits the carriage of precious or semi-precious stones, gold or silver bullion, arms, ammunition, explosives, livestock, animals, plants, and narcotic substances via courier mode. (Source: Courier Imports and Exports Regulations, 2010)
CorrectText: Precious stones, gold or silver in bullion, arms and ammunition, and live animals
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Prohibited Cargo by Courier

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 127B of the Customs Act, 1962, which of the following is a mandatory prerequisite for an applicant to file an application before the Customs Settlement Commission?
OptionA: The applicant must deposit 100% penalty before applying
OptionB: The additional amount of customs duty accepted by the applicant in the application must exceed Rs 3 Lakhs, and the applicant must have filed a Bill of Entry/Shipping Bill and received an SCN
OptionC: The applicant must have already been convicted by a criminal court
OptionD: The case must involve contraband gold seized on person
Explanation: Section 127B mandates that the applicant must have filed a Bill of Entry/Shipping Bill, received a Show Cause Notice, made full and true disclosure, admitted additional duty liability exceeding Rs 3 Lakhs, and paid such duty with interest. (Source: Section 127B Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The additional amount of customs duty accepted by the applicant in the application must exceed Rs 3 Lakhs, and the applicant must have filed a Bill of Entry/Shipping Bill and received an SCN
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 127B - Eligibility Criteria

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: What statutory immunity can the Customs Settlement Commission grant under Section 127H of the Customs Act, 1962 upon being satisfied with full cooperation by the applicant?
OptionA: Immunity from payment of Basic Customs Duty
OptionB: Immunity from complying with FSSAI regulations
OptionC: Immunity from GST audits for 10 years
OptionD: Immunity from prosecution for any offence under the Customs Act or IPC in relation to the case, and immunity from whole or part of any penalty and fine
Explanation: Section 127H empowers the Settlement Commission to grant immunity from prosecution for any offence under the Customs Act or Indian Penal Code, as well as from the imposition of whole or any part of penalties and fines. (Source: Section 127H Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Immunity from prosecution for any offence under the Customs Act or IPC in relation to the case, and immunity from whole or part of any penalty and fine
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 127H - Power to Grant Immunity

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Section: Section 30 of SEZ Act - DTA Sales
Question: Under Section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, when goods manufactured or produced in an SEZ are cleared into the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA), customs duty is chargeable at what rate?
OptionB: At the rates of customs duties, including BCD and IGST, as are leviable on import of such goods into India from outside India
OptionC: At the internal state VAT rate only
OptionD: Completely free of all customs duty since manufacture occurred within India
Explanation: Section 30 of the SEZ Act provides that any goods removed or cleared from an SEZ into the DTA shall be chargeable to customs duty, including anti-dumping, countervailing, and safeguard duties, as are leviable on such goods when imported into India. (Source: Section 30 SEZ Act, 2005)
CorrectText: At the rates of customs duties, including BCD and IGST, as are leviable on import of such goods into India from outside India
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 30 of SEZ Act - DTA Sales

Chapter: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests
Question: Under the Sea Cargo Manifest and Transhipment Regulations, 2018 (SCMTR), what is a 'PCIN' (Pre-Cargo Information Number)?
OptionA: A vessel tracking transponder frequency code
OptionB: A unique identifier generated by ICEGATE upon submission of cargo details by the freight forwarder / cargo aggregator before vessel departure from origin port
OptionC: A port parking slot booking number
OptionD: A customs officer's digital signature key
Explanation: Under SCMTR 2018, PCIN is the Pre-Cargo Information Number generated by the customs system when cargo details are filed electronically by the consignor/freight forwarder prior to departure of the vessel from the load port. (Source: SCMTR 2018 / CBIC Guidelines)
CorrectText: A unique identifier generated by ICEGATE upon submission of cargo details by the freight forwarder / cargo aggregator before vessel departure from origin port
Topic: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests — Sea Arrival Manifest (SAM) & PCIN

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: How is assessable value determined for customs clearance of imported goods purchased on a High Sea Sale (HSS) basis?
OptionA: Always by adding flat 10% HSS commission to original invoice
OptionB: Always on the original manufacturer invoice only, ignoring the HSS contract price
OptionC: On the basis of the actual High Sea Sale contract price paid by the final high sea buyer (which includes original CIF value plus high sea sale margin/profit), provided it reflects genuine commercial transaction value
OptionD: By deducting ocean freight from the purchase invoice
Explanation: Under Section 14 and CBIC instructions, assessable value for HSS transactions is the actual price paid by the high sea buyer to the high sea seller (inclusive of HSS margin/profit), reflecting the price at the time and place of importation. (Source: CBIC Circulars / R.K. Jain)
CorrectText: On the basis of the actual High Sea Sale contract price paid by the final high sea buyer (which includes original CIF value plus high sea sale margin/profit), provided it reflects genuine commercial transaction value
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Valuation of High Sea Sales

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under the IPR (Imported Goods) Enforcement Rules, 2007, when Customs suspends clearance of suspected counterfeit goods upon notice by the right holder, within what time period must the right holder join proceedings and execute the requisite bond and bank guarantee?
OptionC: 10 working days (3 working days in case of perishable goods)
Explanation: Rule 7(1) of IPR Rules 2007 mandates that the right holder must join proceedings within 10 working days (or 3 working days for perishable goods) of being notified of suspension of clearance, failing which the goods shall be released. (Source: Rule 7 IPR Rules, 2007)
CorrectText: 10 working days (3 working days in case of perishable goods)
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 5 & Rule 7 - Suspension of Clearance

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under Rule 9 of the IPR (Imported Goods) Enforcement Rules, 2007, how must confiscated counterfeit trademark goods be treated?
OptionA: They must be sold through customs public auction after removing outer cartons only
OptionB: They shall be destroyed or disposed of outside the channels of commerce, and cannot be allowed to be re-exported in an unaltered state
OptionC: They can be re-exported in their original state to the manufacturer
OptionD: They must be gifted to customs officers
Explanation: Rule 9 prohibits allowing confiscated counterfeit goods to be re-exported in an unaltered state; they must be destroyed under customs supervision or disposed of outside commercial channels with right holder concurrence. (Source: Rule 9 IPR Rules, 2007)
CorrectText: They shall be destroyed or disposed of outside the channels of commerce, and cannot be allowed to be re-exported in an unaltered state
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Disposal of Confiscated Counterfeit Goods

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under the Foreign Trade Policy conditions for import of brand-new passenger cars, which of the following is a mandatory technical and homologation compliance requirement?
OptionA: The vehicle must have an engine capacity exceeding 5000cc exclusively
OptionB: The vehicle must have right-hand steering, speedometer calibrated in km/h, and a homologation road-worthiness certificate issued by ARAI/VRDE/ICAT
OptionC: The vehicle must be left-hand drive
OptionD: No homologation is required if imported by air
Explanation: Chapter 87 Policy Conditions mandate that new imported vehicles must be right-hand drive, have speedometers in km/h, meet photometric and emissions standards, and submit a type-approval certificate from designated testing agencies like ARAI or ICAT. (Source: Chapter 87 ITC(HS) Policy)
CorrectText: The vehicle must have right-hand steering, speedometer calibrated in km/h, and a homologation road-worthiness certificate issued by ARAI/VRDE/ICAT
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Policy Condition 1 of Chapter 87

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: What is the statutory requirement for import of un-shredded metallic waste and scrap into India under the Foreign Trade Policy?
OptionA: Import of metallic scrap is completely banned in India
OptionB: It can enter through any small land customs station without inspection
OptionC: It requires a Pre-Shipment Inspection Certificate (PSIC) from a DGFT-approved agency certifying that the consignment contains no arms, ammunition, mines, or radiation, and must enter through designated ports equipped with Radiation Portal Monitors
OptionD: It requires approval from the Reserve Bank of India
Explanation: Paragraph 2.54 of HBP mandates that un-shredded scrap must be accompanied by a PSIC from an approved inspection agency certifying absence of explosives, shells, and radioactive contamination, and can clear only through designated ports with portal radiation monitors. (Source: FTP 2023 HBP Para 2.54)
CorrectText: It requires a Pre-Shipment Inspection Certificate (PSIC) from a DGFT-approved agency certifying that the consignment contains no arms, ammunition, mines, or radiation, and must enter through designated ports equipped with Radiation Portal Monitors
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Pre-Shipment Inspection Certificate (PSIC)

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 123 of the Customs Act, 1962, when specified goods (such as gold, bullion, watches, diamonds, synthetic yarn, cigarettes) are seized in the reasonable belief that they are smuggled goods, on whom does the burden of proving that they are NOT smuggled goods rest?
OptionA: On the manufacturer in the foreign country
OptionB: Strictly on the Customs Appraising Officer who seized them
OptionD: On the person from whose possession the goods were seized, or any person who claims to be the owner thereof
Explanation: Section 123 is a statutory exception to normal criminal jurisprudence: the burden of proving that the seized goods are not smuggled goods lies squarely on the person from whose possession they were seized. (Source: Section 123 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: On the person from whose possession the goods were seized, or any person who claims to be the owner thereof
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 123 - Burden of Proof

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 102(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, when an officer is about to search any person under Section 100 or 101, what mandatory right must the officer inform the person of?
OptionA: The right to be taken without unnecessary delay before the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate
OptionB: The right to refuse search unconditionally
OptionC: The right to immediate legal representation before the Supreme Court
OptionD: The right to claim cash compensation on the spot
Explanation: Section 102(1) mandates that the officer about to search a person shall inform him that he has the right to be taken before the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate. (Source: Section 102 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The right to be taken without unnecessary delay before the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 102 - Search of Persons

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 110(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, where goods are seized by customs and no Show Cause Notice is given under Section 124 within what time period (extendable by up to 6 months by Principal Commissioner), must the seized goods be returned to the person from whose possession they were seized?
OptionA: 6 months from the date of seizure
Explanation: Section 110(2) provides that where any goods are seized and no notice under Section 124(a) is given within six months (or extended six months by Principal Commissioner upon sufficient cause), the goods shall be returned to the person from whom seized. (Source: Section 110(2) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 6 months from the date of seizure
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 110(2) - Seizure Notice Timeline

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 110A of the Customs Act, 1962, how may any goods, documents or conveyances seized under Section 110 be provisionally released to the owner pending adjudication?
OptionA: Provisional release is prohibited under Indian law
OptionB: Only upon payment of full redemption fine in cash upfront
OptionC: By obtaining an order from the local municipal panchayat
OptionD: Upon execution by the owner of a bond with such security or bank guarantee as the adjudicating authority may require
Explanation: Section 110A empowers the adjudicating authority to release seized goods, documents, or conveyances provisionally to the owner on taking a bond in the proper form with appropriate security/bank guarantee. (Source: Section 110A Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Upon execution by the owner of a bond with such security or bank guarantee as the adjudicating authority may require
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 110A - Provisional Release

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 115(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, when is a conveyance (truck, vessel, aircraft) used in the smuggling of goods NOT liable to confiscation?
OptionA: If the cargo value is less than the truck value
OptionB: If the driver was driving below the speed limit
OptionC: If the conveyance is owned by a foreign company
OptionD: If the owner proves that it was so used without the knowledge or connivance of the owner himself, his agent, and the person-in-charge, and each of them had taken all reasonable precautions
Explanation: Section 115(2) provides that a conveyance shall not be confiscated if the owner proves that it was used without knowledge or connivance of the owner, agent, or master, and that all reasonable precautions had been taken. (Source: Section 115(2) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: If the owner proves that it was so used without the knowledge or connivance of the owner himself, his agent, and the person-in-charge, and each of them had taken all reasonable precautions
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 115 - Confiscation of Conveyances

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Section: Section 121 - Sale Proceeds of Smuggled Goods
Question: Under Section 121 of the Customs Act, 1962, where any smuggled goods are sold by a person having knowledge or reason to believe that the goods are smuggled goods, what can customs confiscate?
OptionD: Nothing, once the goods have changed hands
Explanation: Section 121 provides that where any smuggled goods are sold by a person with knowledge or reason to believe they are smuggled, the sale-proceeds thereof shall be liable to confiscation. (Source: Section 121 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The sale-proceeds thereof
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 121 - Sale Proceeds of Smuggled Goods

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Section 149 of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the crucial legal restriction on amending a Bill of Entry or Shipping Bill AFTER the goods have been cleared for home consumption or for export?
OptionA: Amendments can be made only with prior permission of the Reserve Bank of India
OptionB: Amendments can be made freely within 5 years without proof
OptionC: No amendment is ever permitted under any circumstance
OptionD: No amendment shall be allowed except on the basis of documentary evidence which was in existence at the time the goods were cleared, deposited, or exported
Explanation: The proviso to Section 149 strictly bars any amendment of an entry after clearance, except on the basis of documentary evidence which was in existence at the time the goods were cleared, deposited, or exported. (Source: Section 149 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: No amendment shall be allowed except on the basis of documentary evidence which was in existence at the time the goods were cleared, deposited, or exported
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 149 - Amendment of Documents

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Which national online infrastructure operates as the notified 'Common Customs Electronic Portal' under Section 154C of the Customs Act, 1962 for filing registrations, declarations, and service of orders?
Explanation: Under Section 154C, the Central Government notified the ICEGATE portal (www.icegate.gov.in) as the Common Customs Electronic Portal for paperless processing, electronic declarations, and digital service of notices. (Source: Section 154C Customs Act / Notif 33/2021-Cus (N.T.))
CorrectText: ICEGATE (Indian Customs Electronic Gateway)
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 154C - Common Customs Electronic Portal

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Section: Section 155 - Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith
Question: What statutory protection does Section 155 of the Customs Act, 1962 afford to customs officers and Central Government personnel?
OptionA: No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Central Government or any customs officer for anything done or intended to be done in good faith in pursuance of the Act
OptionB: Automatic promotion upon completing five years of service
OptionC: Absolute immunity from criminal law for any deliberate corruption
Explanation: Section 155(1) protects the Central Government and officers from civil suits or criminal prosecutions for acts done or intended to be done in good faith in pursuance of the Act or rules. (Source: Section 155 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Central Government or any customs officer for anything done or intended to be done in good faith in pursuance of the Act
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 155 - Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Section: Regulation 13 - Form G & Form F Cards
Question: Under Regulation 13 of CBLR, 2018, which identity card is issued to an employee/assistant of a Customs Broker who has passed the examination conducted under Regulation 13(5)?
Explanation: Regulation 13(5) provides that an employee who qualifies in the examination conducted by customs is issued a photo identity card in Form G, authorizing him to sign customs documents and transact business on behalf of the broker. (Source: Regulation 13 CBLR, 2018)
CorrectText: Form G Card
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 13 - Form G & Form F Cards

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 18 of CBLR, 2018, what is the maximum financial penalty that the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs can impose on a Customs Broker for contravention of any provision of the regulations?
Explanation: Regulation 18 empowers the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs to impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees (Rs 50,000) on a Customs Broker for failure to comply with any provision of CBLR 2018. (Source: Regulation 18 CBLR, 2018)
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 18 - Penalty on Customs Broker

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 10(f) of CBLR, 2018, for what minimum period is a Customs Broker statutorily required to maintain and preserve all records and accounts relating to customs transactions?
Explanation: Regulation 10(f) mandates that a Customs Broker must maintain up to date all records, accounts and documents for a period of not less than five years, and produce them before the proper officer upon inspection. (Source: Regulation 10(f) CBLR, 2018)
CorrectText: 5 years
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10(f)

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: What is the fundamental statutory difference between 'Transit' under Section 53 and 'Transhipment' under Section 54 of the Customs Act, 1962?
OptionA: In transit, goods remain on the same conveyance throughout until reaching the destination port; in transhipment, goods are transferred from one conveyance to another conveyance under a transhipment permit and bond without payment of duty
OptionB: Transit applies only to export goods; transhipment applies only to passenger baggage
OptionC: Transit requires payment of full customs duty; transhipment is exempt from all laws
OptionD: Transit applies only to air cargo; transhipment applies only to railway wagons
Explanation: Under Section 53 (Transit), cargo mentioned in the manifest for another port stays on the same vessel/aircraft. Under Section 54 (Transhipment), cargo is unloaded and transferred to another vessel/aircraft/truck under a transhipment permit and bond. (Source: Section 53 & 54 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: In transit, goods remain on the same conveyance throughout until reaching the destination port; in transhipment, goods are transferred from one conveyance to another conveyance under a transhipment permit and bond without payment of duty
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 53 & Section 54

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 3(2) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007, which of the following conditions must be satisfied for the transaction value to be accepted by the proper officer?
OptionA: The buyer and seller must be related in all commercial transactions
OptionB: The payment must be settled exclusively in cash at the port
OptionC: There are no restrictions as to the disposition or use of the goods by the buyer, other than restrictions imposed by Indian law or public authorities, or limiting geographical resale area, or not substantially affecting value
OptionD: The invoice value must be exactly identical to the Directorate of Valuation benchmark
Explanation: Rule 3(2) stipulates four mandatory conditions: (a) no restrictions on disposition/use (except statutory/territorial), (b) sale not subject to unascertainable condition, (c) no proceeds reversion without Rule 10 adjustment, and (d) buyer and seller are not related or price is acceptable under Rule 3(3). (Source: Rule 3(2) CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: There are no restrictions as to the disposition or use of the goods by the buyer, other than restrictions imposed by Indian law or public authorities, or limiting geographical resale area, or not substantially affecting value
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3(2) - Conditions for Transaction Value

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what is a mandatory statutory test for goods to qualify as 'identical goods'?
OptionA: They must be the same in all respects, including physical characteristics, quality, and reputation, and produced in the same country by the same person (or another person if none available)
OptionB: They must be manufactured in any country in the world by any corporation
OptionC: They must have been exported at least 5 years apart
OptionD: They must merely belong to the same 2-digit tariff chapter
Explanation: Rule 2(1)(d) and Rule 4 define 'identical goods' as goods which are the same in all respects, including physical characteristics, quality, and reputation, produced in the same country by the same person who produced the goods being valued (or another producer if none from same producer). (Source: Rule 4 CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: They must be the same in all respects, including physical characteristics, quality, and reputation, and produced in the same country by the same person (or another person if none available)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 4 - Identical Goods Method

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 5 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what defines 'similar goods' for customs appraisal purposes?
OptionA: Goods imported in the same shipping container
OptionB: Goods which, although not alike in all respects, have like characteristics and like component materials which enable them to perform the same functions and to be commercially interchangeable, produced in the same country
OptionC: Goods carrying identical brand trademarks regardless of origin
OptionD: Goods that look visually alike but have entirely different functions
Explanation: Rule 2(1)(f) and Rule 5 define 'similar goods' as goods which have like characteristics and component materials enabling them to perform the same functions and be commercially interchangeable, produced in the same country. (Source: Rule 5 CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: Goods which, although not alike in all respects, have like characteristics and like component materials which enable them to perform the same functions and to be commercially interchangeable, produced in the same country
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 5 - Similar Goods Method

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 7 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007 (Deductive Value Method), what is the starting price point for determining assessable value?
OptionA: The price declared on the shipping bill of previous exports
OptionB: The unit price at which the imported goods (or identical/similar goods) are sold in the greatest aggregate quantity to persons who are not related to the sellers in India at or about the time of importation
OptionC: The replacement manufacturing cost estimated by customs appraisers
OptionD: The retail maximum selling price in the country of exportation
Explanation: Rule 7(1) provides that the value is based on the unit price at which imported goods or identical/similar imported goods are sold in India in the greatest aggregate quantity to unrelated buyers, subject to statutory deductions. (Source: Rule 7 CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: The unit price at which the imported goods (or identical/similar goods) are sold in the greatest aggregate quantity to persons who are not related to the sellers in India at or about the time of importation
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 7 - Deductive Value Method

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007 (Computed Value Method), what components constitute the computed value?
OptionA: The highest price recorded at the London Metal Exchange
OptionB: The cost of materials and fabrication, plus an amount for profit and general expenses equal to that usually reflected in sales of goods of the same class by producers in the country of exportation, plus Rule 10(2) costs
OptionC: Only the freight and insurance paid for transit
OptionD: The retail price in India minus 50% flat discount
Explanation: Rule 8 prescribes that computed value consists of: (a) cost or value of materials and fabrication, (b) profit and general expenses usually reflected in exports to India, and (c) transportation, loading, and insurance costs under Rule 10(2). (Source: Rule 8 CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: The cost of materials and fabrication, plus an amount for profit and general expenses equal to that usually reflected in sales of goods of the same class by producers in the country of exportation, plus Rule 10(2) costs
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 8 - Computed Value Method

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 9 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007 (Residual Method), which of the following valuation bases is EXPRESSLY PROHIBITED from being adopted?
OptionA: The selling price in India of goods produced in India, the price of goods in the domestic market of the exporting country, or arbitrary/fictitious values
OptionC: Reasonable means consistent with the principles of Section 14
OptionD: Data available from previous genuine imports of similar goods
Explanation: Rule 9(2) expressly prohibits: (a) selling price of Indian goods, (b) system where highest value is adopted, (c) domestic market price in country of export, (d) cost of production other than computed values, (e) price for export to a third country, (f) minimum customs values, or (g) arbitrary or fictitious values. (Source: Rule 9(2) CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: The selling price in India of goods produced in India, the price of goods in the domestic market of the exporting country, or arbitrary/fictitious values
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 9 - Residual Method Prohibitions

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 10(1)(a)(i) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, how are 'buying commissions' treated when calculating the customs transaction value?
OptionA: Buying commissions are expressly excluded from being added to the price actually paid or payable
OptionB: Buying commissions must be credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund
OptionC: Buying commissions are subjected to full basic customs duty plus IGST separately
OptionD: Buying commissions must be compulsorily added to invoice value at flat 5%
Explanation: Rule 10(1)(a)(i) states that commissions and brokerage, except buying commissions, incurred by the buyer shall be added to the price paid or payable. Buying commission paid to an agent representing the buyer is not includible. (Source: Rule 10(1)(a)(i) CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: Buying commissions are expressly excluded from being added to the price actually paid or payable
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(1)(a) - Buying Commissions

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 10(1)(b)(iv) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what is the statutory rule regarding the value of engineering, development, artwork, and design work supplied by the buyer?
OptionA: Development work undertaken in India must be taxed at double the value
OptionB: All engineering and design work is includible regardless of where undertaken
OptionC: Assists can only be valued if the supplier is a public sector undertaking
OptionD: The value of such engineering, development, artwork, and design work is includible in assessable value ONLY if undertaken outside India
Explanation: Rule 10(1)(b)(iv) specifies that the value of engineering, development, artwork, design work, and plans and sketches is added only if undertaken elsewhere than in India and is necessary for the production of the imported goods. (Source: Rule 10(1)(b)(iv) CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: The value of such engineering, development, artwork, and design work is includible in assessable value ONLY if undertaken outside India
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(1)(b) - Assists Undertaken in India

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Section: Rule 10(2) - Freight and Insurance Not Ascertainable
Question: Under Rule 10(2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, where the actual cost of transportation and the actual cost of insurance are not ascertainable, how are they computed?
OptionA: Freight @ 5% of FOB; Insurance @ 0.5% of FOB
OptionC: Freight @ 10% of FOB; Insurance @ 2% of FOB
OptionD: Freight @ 20% of FOB value; Insurance @ 1.125% of FOB value
Explanation: Under the proviso to Rule 10(2), if transportation cost is not ascertainable, it shall be 20% of FOB value. If insurance cost is not ascertainable, it shall be 1.125% of FOB value. (Source: Rule 10(2) CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: Freight @ 20% of FOB value; Insurance @ 1.125% of FOB value
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2) - Freight and Insurance Not Ascertainable

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under the third proviso to Rule 10(2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what ceiling applies to the cost of transport for goods imported by air?
OptionA: Air freight can never exceed 10% of CIF value
OptionB: Where goods are imported by air, the transportation cost added shall not exceed 20% of the FOB value of the goods, even if actual air freight incurred is higher
OptionC: Air freight is capped at Rs 100 per kilogram
OptionD: There is no ceiling; actual air freight must always be added in full
Explanation: The proviso to Rule 10(2)(a) specifically mandates that in the case of goods imported by air, the cost of transport, loading, unloading, and handling charges shall not exceed 20% of the FOB value of the goods. (Source: Rule 10(2) CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: Where goods are imported by air, the transportation cost added shall not exceed 20% of the FOB value of the goods, even if actual air freight incurred is higher
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2) - Air Freight Limitation

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 12 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what procedure must the proper officer follow before rejecting the declared transaction value?
OptionA: The officer must have reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of declared value, intimate the grounds of doubt in writing, give reasonable opportunity of being heard, and record reasons for rejection
OptionB: The officer must obtain approval from the Ministry of External Affairs
OptionC: The officer can issue a confiscation order instantly without any explanation
OptionD: The officer must demand 50% deposit before raising any query
Explanation: Rule 12 mandates that where the proper officer has reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of declared value, he shall ask the importer for further information, intimate grounds of doubt, provide reasonable opportunity of being heard, and record reasons in writing. (Source: Rule 12 CVR, 2007)
CorrectText: The officer must have reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of declared value, intimate the grounds of doubt in writing, give reasonable opportunity of being heard, and record reasons for rejection
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 12 - Rejection of Declared Value

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 28(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the normal statutory time limit for the proper officer to serve a Show Cause Notice for non-levy, short-levy, or erroneous refund not involving collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts?
OptionC: 2 years from the relevant date (amended from 1 year by Finance Act, 2016)
Explanation: Section 28(1)(a) provides that in normal cases not involving collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts, the proper officer shall serve a notice within two years from the relevant date. (Source: Section 28(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 2 years from the relevant date (amended from 1 year by Finance Act, 2016)
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(1) - Normal Limitation Period

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 28(4) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the extended limitation period to issue a Show Cause Notice where duty has not been levied or has been short-levied by reason of collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts?
Explanation: Section 28(4) provides an extended limitation period of five years from the relevant date where duty has not been levied, short-levied, or erroneously refunded by reason of collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts. (Source: Section 28(4) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 5 years from the relevant date
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(4) - Extended Limitation Period

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Section: Section 28(5) - Reduced Penalty on Early Payment
Question: Under Section 28(5) of the Customs Act, 1962, where a notice is issued under Section 28(4) (extended period) and the noticee pays the duty, interest, and penalty within 30 days of receipt of the notice, what is the concessional penalty payable?
OptionC: 25% of the penalty specified in the notice
Explanation: Under Section 28(5), where any person to whom a notice is served under Section 28(4) pays the duty in full, interest under Section 28AA, and a penalty equal to 15% of the duty within 30 days of receipt of the notice, proceedings in respect of such duty shall be deemed to be concluded. (Source: Section 28(5) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 15% of the duty amount
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(5) - Reduced Penalty on Early Payment

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Section: Section 28AA - Interest on Delayed Payment of Duty
Question: Under Section 28AA of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the statutory rate of interest notified by the Central Government on delayed payment of customs duty?
Explanation: Under Section 28AA read with Notification No. 33/2016-Customs (N.T.), the Central Government has fixed the rate of interest on delayed payment of customs duty at 15% per annum from the date specified under the Act till actual payment. (Source: Section 28AA / Notif 33/2016-Cus (N.T.))
CorrectText: 15% per annum
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28AA - Interest on Delayed Payment of Duty

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 281B of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the initial statutory validity period of an order of provisional attachment of property passed to protect revenue during pendency of recovery proceedings?
OptionC: 6 months (extendable by Principal Commissioner for reasons recorded in writing, total period not exceeding 2 years)
Explanation: Section 281B(2) provides that every order of provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of six months, subject to extension by the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner for reasons recorded in writing up to a total maximum of two years. (Source: Section 281B Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 6 months (extendable by Principal Commissioner for reasons recorded in writing, total period not exceeding 2 years)
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 281B - Provisional Attachment

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 112(a)(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the maximum penalty leviable on a person in case of improper importation of PROHIBITED goods?
OptionA: Flat penalty equal to 10% of CIF value
OptionB: Penalty not exceeding twice the ocean freight
OptionC: Penalty not exceeding the value of the goods or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater
Explanation: Section 112(a)(i) provides that in the case of goods in respect of which any prohibition is in force under the Act or any other law, the penalty shall not exceed the value of the goods or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater. (Source: Section 112(a)(i) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Penalty not exceeding the value of the goods or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 112(a) - Penalty for Improper Importation

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 112(a)(ii) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the maximum penalty in case of improper importation of dutiable goods (other than prohibited goods)?
OptionB: Penalty not exceeding ten percent of the duty sought to be evaded or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater
OptionC: Penalty not exceeding five times the market price
Explanation: Section 112(a)(ii) provides that in the case of dutiable goods, other than prohibited goods, the penalty shall not exceed ten percent of the duty sought to be evaded or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater. (Source: Section 112(a)(ii) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Penalty not exceeding ten percent of the duty sought to be evaded or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 112(a)(ii) - Penalty for Dutiable Goods

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 114A of the Customs Act, 1962, where duty has not been levied or has been short-levied by reason of collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts, what is the quantum of penalty determined?
OptionA: Penalty equal to 50% of the FOB export value
OptionB: Discretionary penalty between Rs 1,000 and Rs 5,000
OptionC: A mandatory penalty equal to the duty or interest so determined (reduced to 25% if duty, interest, and penalty are paid within 30 days of receipt of order)
OptionD: No penalty is leviable if the person is a first-time importer
Explanation: Section 114A imposes a mandatory penalty equal to the duty or interest determined under Section 28(8). The first proviso reduces this penalty to 25% if the duty, interest, and reduced penalty are paid within 30 days of the communication of the order. (Source: Section 114A Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: A mandatory penalty equal to the duty or interest so determined (reduced to 25% if duty, interest, and penalty are paid within 30 days of receipt of order)
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114A - Mandatory Penalty for Fraud

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 114AA of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the maximum penalty leviable on a person who knowingly or intentionally makes, signs, or uses any false or incorrect declaration, statement, or document in the transaction of any customs business?
OptionB: Penalty equal to 1% of the invoice value
OptionD: Penalty not exceeding five times the value of goods
Explanation: Section 114AA prescribes that if a person knowingly or intentionally makes, signs, or uses any declaration, statement, or document which is false or incorrect in any material particular, he shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five times the value of goods. (Source: Section 114AA Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Penalty not exceeding five times the value of goods
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114AA - False Declarations and Invoices

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 117 of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the maximum residual penalty for any person who contravenes any provision of the Act or fails to comply with any provision where no express penalty is elsewhere provided?
OptionD: Rs 4,00,000 (amended from Rs 1,00,000 by Finance Act, 2019)
Explanation: Section 117 provides a general penalty for contraventions where no express penalty is provided in the Act, with a maximum ceiling of up to four lakh rupees (Rs 4,00,000), increased from Rs 1,00,000 by Finance Act, 2019. (Source: Section 117 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Rs 4,00,000 (amended from Rs 1,00,000 by Finance Act, 2019)
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 117 - General Penalty

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 125(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the statutory ceiling on the fine that may be imposed in lieu of confiscation (Redemption Fine)?
OptionA: The fine is fixed at a flat Rs 25,000 across all commodities
OptionB: The fine cannot exceed 50% of the assessable value
OptionC: The redemption fine cannot exceed the CIF value of the goods
OptionD: The fine shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less in the case of imported goods the duty chargeable thereon
Explanation: The proviso to Section 125(1) mandates that the redemption fine shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less in the case of imported goods the customs duty chargeable thereon. (Source: Section 125(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The fine shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less in the case of imported goods the duty chargeable thereon
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 125 - Redemption Fine

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 58A of the Customs Act, 1962, which category of goods is statutorily required to be deposited only in a 'Special Warehouse' licensed under this section?
OptionB: General iron and steel structural coils
OptionC: Sensitive goods notified by the Board, including gold, silver, precious stones, duty-free shop goods, and ship stores/aircraft stores under physical customs lock
Explanation: Section 58A(1) read with the Special Warehouse Licensing Regulations, 2016 applies to sensitive goods notified by CBIC, such as gold, silver, duty-free shop merchandise, and ship/airline stores, requiring physical customs lock and control. (Source: Section 58A Customs Act / Notif 66/2016-Cus (N.T.))
CorrectText: Sensitive goods notified by the Board, including gold, silver, precious stones, duty-free shop goods, and ship stores/aircraft stores under physical customs lock
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 58A - Special Warehouses

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 59(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, for what sum must the importer execute a warehousing bond before warehoused goods are allowed to be deposited in a warehouse?
OptionA: A sum equal to thrice (three times) the amount of the duty assessed on the goods
OptionB: A sum equal to twice the amount of duty assessed
OptionC: A sum equal to the duty assessed
OptionD: A sum equal to the total CIF value of the shipment
Explanation: Section 59(1) mandates that the importer shall execute a bond in a sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed on the goods, binding himself to observe all provisions and pay all duties, interest, and charges. (Source: Section 59(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: A sum equal to thrice (three times) the amount of the duty assessed on the goods
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 59 - Warehousing Bond Multiplier

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 61(1)(c) of the Customs Act, 1962, for what period may general imported goods (other than capital goods or inputs for EOUs/MOOWR) remain warehoused in a licensed warehouse?
OptionA: One year from the date of the order made under Section 60 (extendable by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner for up to 1 year at a time)
Explanation: Section 61(1)(c) specifies that in the case of any other goods, they may remain in the warehouse till the expiry of one year from the date of the order permitting deposit under Section 60, subject to extension by the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner. (Source: Section 61(1)(c) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: One year from the date of the order made under Section 60 (extendable by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner for up to 1 year at a time)
