Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 61(1) - Permissible Warehousing Period

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 61(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, where general warehoused goods remain in the warehouse beyond what initial period is interest payable on the customs duty till clearance?
OptionC: Interest is never charged on warehoused goods
OptionD: After the expiry of ninety (90) days from the date of the order permitting deposit under Section 60
Explanation: Section 61(2) provides that where any goods specified in Section 61(1)(c) remain in a warehouse beyond a period of ninety days, interest @ 15% per annum shall be payable on the amount of duty from the expiry of the said ninety days till clearance. (Source: Section 61(2) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: After the expiry of ninety (90) days from the date of the order permitting deposit under Section 60
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 61(2) - Interest on Warehoused Goods

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 65 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with MOOWR Regulations, 2019, what is the customs duty liability when goods manufactured in a bonded warehouse are cleared for export outside India?
OptionA: A flat export surcharge of 10% is levied
OptionB: Duty must be paid and then claimed as drawback after 2 years
OptionC: No customs duty is payable on the imported raw materials or capital goods contained in or used for manufacturing the exported goods (duty remitted)
OptionD: Full customs duty is payable on all raw materials and machinery
Explanation: Under Section 65 and MOOWR Scheme 2019, if resultant products are exported, import duties on the inputs utilized in manufacturing are completely remitted, and no duty is paid on capital goods used in the warehouse. (Source: Section 65 Customs Act / MOOWR Regs 2019)
CorrectText: No customs duty is payable on the imported raw materials or capital goods contained in or used for manufacturing the exported goods (duty remitted)
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 65 - Manufacture in Warehouse (MOOWR)

Chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
Question: Under Section 68 of the Customs Act, 1962, what document must be presented for clearance of warehoused goods for home consumption?
OptionB: Bill of Entry for Ex-Bond Clearance (Green Form) accompanied by payment of duty, interest, and warehouse charges
OptionD: Bill of Entry for Home Consumption (White Form)
Explanation: Section 68 requires the importer to present an Ex-Bond Bill of Entry (traditionally on green paper) for home consumption and pay the assessed import duty, penalties, interest, and storage charges before clearance order is made. (Source: Section 68 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Bill of Entry for Ex-Bond Clearance (Green Form) accompanied by payment of duty, interest, and warehouse charges
Topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 68 - Ex-Bond Bill of Entry

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 128(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, within what time period from the date of communication of an adjudication order (passed by an officer lower than Commissioner) must an appeal be filed before the Commissioner (Appeals)?
OptionD: 60 days from the date of communication (extendable by a further period of 30 days by Commissioner (Appeals) on sufficient cause)
Explanation: Section 128(1) provides that any person aggrieved by any decision or order may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) within sixty days. The proviso permits condonation of delay by a further period of thirty days if satisfied with sufficient cause. (Source: Section 128 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 60 days from the date of communication (extendable by a further period of 30 days by Commissioner (Appeals) on sufficient cause)
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 128 - Appeal to Commissioner (Appeals)

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 129E of the Customs Act, 1962, what percentage of the duty or penalty in dispute must be mandatorily pre-deposited for an appeal before Commissioner (Appeals) and CESTAT respectively?
OptionA: Commissioner (Appeals): 7.5%; CESTAT: 7.5% (for first stage) and 10% (for second stage against Commissioner (Appeals) order), subject to Rs 10 Crore ceiling
Explanation: Section 129E mandates a pre-deposit of: (i) 7.5% of duty/penalty for appeal before Commissioner (Appeals), (ii) 7.5% for appeal before CESTAT against an order of Commissioner, and (iii) 10% for appeal before CESTAT against an order of Commissioner (Appeals), capped at Rs 10 Crores. (Source: Section 129E Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Commissioner (Appeals): 7.5%; CESTAT: 7.5% (for first stage) and 10% (for second stage against Commissioner (Appeals) order), subject to Rs 10 Crore ceiling
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129E - Mandatory Pre-Deposit

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under the proviso to Section 129A(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, CESTAT may in its discretion refuse to admit an appeal where the duty or penalty involved does not exceed what threshold?
Explanation: The second proviso to Section 129A(1) empowers the Appellate Tribunal in its discretion to refuse to admit an appeal where the amount of duty, fine, or penalty determined by the order does not exceed two lakh rupees (Rs 2,00,000). (Source: Section 129A(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Rs 50,000 (amended to Rs 2,00,000)
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129A - CESTAT Monetary Limit

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under the first proviso to Section 129A(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, which types of orders passed by Commissioner (Appeals) CANNOT be appealed before CESTAT, and are instead subject to Revision under Section 129DD?
OptionA: Orders relating to baggage clearance, short-landing/short-shipment of goods, and payment of drawback under Chapter X
OptionB: Orders relating to classification of high-tech semiconductors
OptionD: Orders relating to SEZ DTA sales
Explanation: Under Section 129A(1) first proviso, no appeal lies to CESTAT from an order of Commissioner (Appeals) relating to: (a) goods imported/exported as baggage, (b) short-landing of goods, and (c) duty drawback. These are subject to Revision Application before the Central Government under Section 129DD. (Source: Section 129A(1) & 129DD Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Orders relating to baggage clearance, short-landing/short-shipment of goods, and payment of drawback under Chapter X
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129A - Matched Revision Cases

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 130 of the Customs Act, 1962, on what grounds does an appeal lie from an order of CESTAT to the High Court?
OptionA: CESTAT orders are final and cannot be appealed anywhere
OptionB: Only if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law (not being an order relating to determination of rate of duty or value for purposes of assessment)
OptionC: On any minor factual disagreement regarding dock tally
OptionD: On grounds of delay in translation of documents
Explanation: Section 130(1) allows an appeal to the High Court from every order of the Appellate Tribunal on a substantial question of law, provided the order does not relate to determination of the rate of duty or value of goods for assessment (which go directly to the Supreme Court under Section 130E). (Source: Section 130 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Only if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law (not being an order relating to determination of rate of duty or value for purposes of assessment)
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 130 - Appeal to High Court

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 104 of the Customs Act, 1962, when is an offence under Section 135 cognizable and non-bailable?
OptionA: Only if the person refuses to sign an attendance register
OptionB: All customs offences are always cognizable and non-bailable regardless of amount
OptionC: Customs offences are never non-bailable under any circumstances
OptionD: Offences relating to evasion of duty exceeding Rs 50 Lakhs, or prohibited goods under Section 11, or fraudulent drawback exceeding Rs 50 Lakhs, or specified sensitive goods (gold/firearms) are non-bailable
Explanation: Under Section 104(6), offences punishable under Section 135 relating to: (a) prohibited goods, (b) evasion of duty or fraudulent drawback exceeding Rs 50 Lakhs, or (c) fraudulently availing exemption exceeding Rs 50 Lakhs are non-bailable and cognizable. (Source: Section 104(6) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Offences relating to evasion of duty exceeding Rs 50 Lakhs, or prohibited goods under Section 11, or fraudulent drawback exceeding Rs 50 Lakhs, or specified sensitive goods (gold/firearms) are non-bailable
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 104 - Power to Arrest & Bail

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 135(1)(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the maximum term of imprisonment for evasion of customs duty or misdeclaration where the market price of goods or duty evaded exceeds Rs 50 Lakhs?
OptionA: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven (7) years and with fine (minimum three years imprisonment in absence of special reasons)
Explanation: Section 135(1)(i) provides that where the offence involves prohibited goods or duty evaded or market price exceeding fifty lakh rupees, the person shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and with fine. (Source: Section 135(1)(i) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven (7) years and with fine (minimum three years imprisonment in absence of special reasons)
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 135 - Imprisonment Threshold

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 137(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, who is statutorily authorized to sanction criminal prosecution for offences under Sections 132 to 135A?
OptionA: Any Inspector or Appraiser on port duty
OptionB: The Chairman of Port Trust Authority
OptionC: The State Minister for Home Affairs
OptionD: The Principal Commissioner of Customs or Commissioner of Customs
Explanation: Section 137(1) mandates that no court shall take cognizance of any offence under Sections 132, 133, 134, 135, or 135A, except with the previous sanction of the Principal Commissioner of Customs or Commissioner of Customs. (Source: Section 137(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The Principal Commissioner of Customs or Commissioner of Customs
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 137 - Sanction for Prosecution

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 137(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Customs (Compounding of Offences) Rules, 2005, what is the legal effect of compounding an offence?
OptionA: Compounding does not affect criminal proceedings
OptionB: The goods are destroyed by the military
OptionC: On payment of the compounding amount determined by the Chief Commissioner, criminal proceedings pending in court against the offender abate and terminate completely
OptionD: The offender is barred from importing goods for life
Explanation: Section 137(3) read with Compounding Rules 2005 provides that upon payment of the compounding amount determined by the compounding authority, any criminal proceedings in respect of the compounded offence shall abate and no prosecution can be instituted. (Source: Section 137(3) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: On payment of the compounding amount determined by the Chief Commissioner, criminal proceedings pending in court against the offender abate and terminate completely
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 137(3) - Compounding of Offences

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Section: Rule 1 - Terms of Headings and Notes
Question: Under Rule 1 of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, what is the legal status of titles of Sections, Chapters, and Sub-Chapters?
OptionA: They have binding legal force and override heading text
OptionB: They are meant only for port labor unions
OptionC: They determine the rate of IGST exclusively
OptionD: They are provided for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes
Explanation: Rule 1 explicitly states that the titles of Sections, Chapters and Sub-Chapters are provided for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes. (Source: GIR Rule 1 / Customs Tariff Act, 1975)
CorrectText: They are provided for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 1 - Terms of Headings and Notes

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 2(a) of the General Rules for Interpretation, how is an incomplete or unfinished article classified if, as presented, it has the essential character of the complete or finished article?
OptionA: It shall be classified under the same heading as the complete or finished article, including when presented unassembled or disassembled (CKD/SKD)
OptionB: It must be classified under Chapter 98 as Project Imports
OptionC: It cannot be classified until completely assembled in India
Explanation: Rule 2(a) provides that any reference in a heading to an article shall be taken to include a reference to that article incomplete or unfinished, provided that, as presented, the incomplete or unfinished article has the essential character of the complete or finished article, including knocked down condition. (Source: GIR Rule 2(a))
CorrectText: It shall be classified under the same heading as the complete or finished article, including when presented unassembled or disassembled (CKD/SKD)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 2(a) - Incomplete and Unassembled Articles

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 3(a) of the General Rules for Interpretation, when goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, which principle governs?
OptionA: The heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description
OptionB: The heading with the lowest duty rate must be chosen
OptionC: The heading with the highest alphanumeric number must be chosen
OptionD: The importer can choose any heading at will
Explanation: Rule 3(a) provides that the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description. (Source: GIR Rule 3(a) / Customs Tariff Act, 1975)
CorrectText: The heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3(a) - Specific over General Description

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 3(b) of the General Rules for Interpretation, how are mixtures, composite goods consisting of different materials, and goods put up in sets for retail sale classified?
OptionA: By taking an arithmetic average of all components
OptionB: As if they consisted of the material or component which gives them their 'essential character', insofar as this criterion is applicable
OptionC: Always under the heading for packaging materials
OptionD: Always under the residual heading of Chapter 99
Explanation: Rule 3(b) provides that mixtures, composite goods, and retail sets which cannot be classified by reference to 3(a) shall be classified as if they consisted of the material or component which gives them their essential character. (Source: GIR Rule 3(b))
CorrectText: As if they consisted of the material or component which gives them their 'essential character', insofar as this criterion is applicable
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3(b) - Essential Character Principle

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 3(c) of the General Rules for Interpretation, when goods cannot be classified by reference to Rule 3(a) or 3(b), how shall they be classified?
OptionA: Under the heading which occurs first in numerical order
OptionB: Under the heading suggested by the Chamber of Commerce
OptionD: Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
Explanation: Rule 3(c) explicitly dictates that when goods cannot be classified by reference to Rule 3(a) or 3(b), they shall be classified under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration. (Source: GIR Rule 3(c))
CorrectText: Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3(c) - Last in Numerical Order

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 4 of the General Rules for Interpretation, goods which cannot be classified in accordance with Rules 1, 2, or 3 shall be classified under:
OptionA: Any heading chosen by the port custodian
OptionB: The heading appropriate to the goods to which they are most akin
Explanation: Rule 4 provides that goods which cannot be classified in accordance with Rules 1, 2 or 3 shall be classified under the heading appropriate to the goods to which they are most akin. (Source: GIR Rule 4 / Customs Tariff Act, 1975)
CorrectText: The heading appropriate to the goods to which they are most akin
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 4 - Most Akin Principle

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 5(a) of the General Rules for Interpretation, when are camera cases, musical instrument cases, gun cases, and similar specially fitted containers classified along with the article?
OptionA: Only if imported by diplomatic personnel
OptionB: Fitted cases must always be assessed separately under Chapter 42
OptionC: When specially shaped or fitted to contain a specific article, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles for which they are intended (provided they do not give the whole its essential character)
OptionD: Only if they are manufactured from solid wood
Explanation: Rule 5(a) provides that cases and containers specially shaped/fitted, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles shall be classified with such articles, unless the container gives the whole its essential character. (Source: GIR Rule 5(a))
CorrectText: When specially shaped or fitted to contain a specific article, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles for which they are intended (provided they do not give the whole its essential character)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 5(a) - Fitted Cases and Containers

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 5(b) of the General Rules for Interpretation, what is the statutory exception regarding packing containers presented with goods?
OptionA: Paper cartons are always assessed separately
OptionB: All packaging must be incinerated at customs docks
OptionC: Containers must be re-exported within 24 hours
OptionD: Rule 5(b) is not binding when packing materials or packing containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use (such as returnable steel gas cylinders or ISO tanks)
Explanation: Rule 5(b) provides that packing materials and containers presented with goods are classified with them if of a kind normally used, but this provision is not binding when such packing materials or containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use. (Source: GIR Rule 5(b))
CorrectText: Rule 5(b) is not binding when packing materials or packing containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use (such as returnable steel gas cylinders or ISO tanks)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 5(b) - Repetitive Use Containers

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 6 of the General Rules for Interpretation, how must sub-heading classifications be compared for legal purposes?
OptionA: Only sub-headings at the same level are comparable (e.g. single dash with single dash, and double dash with double dash)
OptionB: Sub-heading classification is determined by the municipal corporation
OptionC: Sub-heading rules override Section and Chapter Notes unconditionally
OptionD: Any 6-digit subheading can be compared directly with any 8-digit tariff item
Explanation: Rule 6 specifies that the classification of goods in the sub-headings of a heading shall be determined according to the terms of those sub-headings, and only sub-headings at the same level are comparable. (Source: GIR Rule 6 / Customs Tariff Act, 1975)
CorrectText: Only sub-headings at the same level are comparable (e.g. single dash with single dash, and double dash with double dash)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 6 - Sub-Heading Classification

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Paragraph 1.35 of FTP 2023, what is the standard annual export turnover threshold required for a town to be notified as a Town of Export Excellence (TEE)?
OptionA: Rs 750 Crores (Rs 150 Crores for Handloom, Handicraft, Agriculture, and Fisheries sectors)
Explanation: Paragraph 1.35 provides that towns producing goods of Rs 750 Crores or more may be recognized as TEE based on export potential; however, for Handloom, Handicraft, Agriculture and Fisheries sectors, the threshold is Rs 150 Crores. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 1.35)
CorrectText: Rs 750 Crores (Rs 150 Crores for Handloom, Handicraft, Agriculture, and Fisheries sectors)
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 1.35 - Eligibility Benchmark

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Section 7 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992, what is the statutory status of the Importer-Exporter Code (IEC)?
OptionA: No person shall make any import or export except under an Importer-Exporter Code number granted by the Director General or authorized officer
OptionB: It is an optional marketing number issued by trade associations
OptionC: It is required only for exports to South America
OptionD: It is granted automatically to every citizen on turning 18
Explanation: Section 7 of the FTDR Act, 1992 mandates that no person shall make any import or export except under an Importer-exporter Code Number granted by the Director General or the officer authorised by the Director General. (Source: Section 7 FTDR Act, 1992)
CorrectText: No person shall make any import or export except under an Importer-Exporter Code number granted by the Director General or authorized officer
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 7 - Importer-Exporter Code (IEC)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Section 11(2) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992, what is the statutory financial penalty for contravening any provision of the Act, rules, orders, or FTP?
OptionA: Penalty equal to 100% of the company's net worth
OptionC: A penalty not less than ten thousand rupees and not more than five times the value of the goods or services or technology in respect of which the contravention is made
Explanation: Section 11(2) of the FTDR Act provides that where any person contravenes any provision of the Act, rules or orders, he shall be liable to a penalty of not less than ten thousand rupees and not more than five times the value of goods/services/technology. (Source: Section 11(2) FTDR Act, 1992)
CorrectText: A penalty not less than ten thousand rupees and not more than five times the value of the goods or services or technology in respect of which the contravention is made
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 11(2) - Penalties for Contravention

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Section 15 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992, within what time period must an appeal against an order passed by an Adjudicating Authority be preferred?
OptionC: 45 days from the date on which the decision or order is served
Explanation: Section 15(1) of the FTDR Act provides that any person aggrieved by any decision or order made under the Act may prefer an appeal within forty-five days from the date on which the decision or order is served on him. (Source: Section 15(1) FTDR Act, 1992)
CorrectText: 45 days from the date on which the decision or order is served
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 15 - Appellate Authorities

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Paragraph 4.14 of FTP 2023, what facility can an Advance Authorisation holder avail if they decide to source duty-free inputs from indigenous domestic suppliers instead of direct importation?
OptionA: They can obtain an Advance Release Order (ARO) or Invalidation Letter from the Regional Authority to procure inputs domestically against deemed export benefits
OptionB: They must surrender their GST registration
OptionC: They can procure inputs with cash subsidies from the State Government
OptionD: They must cancel the Advance Authorisation and pay 50% penalty
Explanation: Paragraph 4.14 of FTP 2023 allows an Advance Authorisation holder intending to source inputs from indigenous suppliers to obtain an Advance Release Order (ARO) or Invalidation Letter, treating the supply as deemed exports. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 4.14)
CorrectText: They can obtain an Advance Release Order (ARO) or Invalidation Letter from the Regional Authority to procure inputs domestically against deemed export benefits
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — FTP 2023 Para 4.14 - Advance Release Order (ARO)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Section: FTP 2023 Para 7.02 - Eligible Deemed Export Categories
Question: Under Paragraph 7.02 of FTP 2023, which of the following transactions qualifies as 'Deemed Exports'?
OptionA: Supply of passenger vehicles to private taxi drivers
OptionB: Shipment of personal effects between two domestic cities
OptionC: Supply of goods against Advance Authorisation / DFIA, supply of capital goods to EPCG authorisations, and supplies to Export Oriented Units (EOUs)
OptionD: Sale of goods across retail counters in domestic shopping malls
Explanation: Paragraph 7.02 defines Deemed Exports as supplies of goods manufactured in India where goods do not leave the country, including supplies against Advance Authorisation/DFIA, supplies to EOU/STP/EHTP, and supply of capital goods under EPCG. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 7.02)
CorrectText: Supply of goods against Advance Authorisation / DFIA, supply of capital goods to EPCG authorisations, and supplies to Export Oriented Units (EOUs)
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 7.02 - Eligible Deemed Export Categories

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Chapter 6 of FTP 2023, what is the mandatory financial performance requirement that an Export Oriented Unit (EOU) must achieve over a 5-year block?
OptionA: Minimum gross export of Rs 100 Crores annually
OptionB: A positive Net Foreign Exchange Earnings (NFE) cumulatively, calculated as NFE = FOB value of exports minus CIF value of imported inputs and capital goods amortization
OptionC: Zero domestic clearance throughout the entire 5 years
Explanation: Paragraph 6.04 of FTP 2023 requires that an EOU/EHTP/STP/BTP unit shall achieve positive Net Foreign Exchange Earnings (NFE) cumulatively for a period of five years from the commencement of commercial production. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 6.04)
CorrectText: A positive Net Foreign Exchange Earnings (NFE) cumulatively, calculated as NFE = FOB value of exports minus CIF value of imported inputs and capital goods amortization
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 6.01 - Net Foreign Exchange (NFE)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Paragraph 6.08 of FTP 2023, to what extent can an EOU clear its manufactured goods into the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) against concessional duties upon achieving positive NFE?
OptionA: DTA sales are strictly prohibited for EOUs
OptionB: Up to 50% of the FOB value of physical exports, on payment of applicable duties
OptionC: Up to 10% of FOB value of exports
OptionD: 100% of its production can be sold in DTA unconditionally
Explanation: Paragraph 6.08 of FTP 2023 permits EOUs to sell up to 50% of FOB value of physical exports into the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) on payment of applicable duties, provided the unit maintains positive NFE. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 6.08)
CorrectText: Up to 50% of the FOB value of physical exports, on payment of applicable duties
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 6.08 - DTA Clearance Concessions

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Chapter 4 of FTP 2023, which specific export sectors are eligible for the RoSCTL (Rebate of State and Central Taxes and Levies) Scheme?
OptionA: Only mineral ores and petroleum products
OptionB: Iron and steel bars and billets
OptionD: Apparel and garments (ITC HS Chapters 61 and 62) and Made-up textile articles (ITC HS Chapter 63)
Explanation: The RoSCTL scheme is specifically notified for the export of garments and apparels (Chapters 61 & 62) and made-ups (Chapter 63) to rebate embedded central and state taxes like State VAT, mandi tax, and electricity duty. (Source: FTP 2023 / Ministry of Textiles Notif)
CorrectText: Apparel and garments (ITC HS Chapters 61 and 62) and Made-up textile articles (ITC HS Chapter 63)
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 4.01 - Scope of RoSCTL

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Section: FTP 2023 Para 2.52 - Rupee Invoicing and Vostro Accounts
Question: Under Paragraph 2.52 of FTP 2023 and RBI Circular A.P. (DIR Series) No. 10, how may international trade transactions be settled in Indian Rupees (INR)?
OptionA: By carrying physical Indian currency notes across borders
OptionB: Settlement in INR for foreign trade is prohibited under Indian law
OptionC: Only through barter arrangements of gold coins
OptionD: Through Special Non-Resident Rupee (SNRR) and Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVA) opened by foreign correspondent banks with Authorized Dealer (AD) banks in India
Explanation: Paragraph 2.52 of FTP 2023 and RBI guidelines allow invoicing, payment, and settlement of exports and imports in INR through Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVA) maintained by partner trading country banks with authorized dealer banks in India. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 2.52 / RBI Circular 10/2022)
CorrectText: Through Special Non-Resident Rupee (SNRR) and Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVA) opened by foreign correspondent banks with Authorized Dealer (AD) banks in India
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 2.52 - Rupee Invoicing and Vostro Accounts

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Paragraph 9.04 of FTP 2023, what is the enhanced consignment value ceiling for exports through courier mode to qualify for e-commerce export facilitation and FTP benefits?
OptionA: Rs 10 Lakhs per consignment (increased from Rs 5 Lakhs)
Explanation: FTP 2023 increased the consignment value limit for exports through courier from Rs 5 Lakhs to Rs 10 Lakhs per consignment to foster growth in cross-border e-commerce exports. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 9.04)
CorrectText: Rs 10 Lakhs per consignment (increased from Rs 5 Lakhs)
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 9.04 - Consignment Value Limit

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Paragraph 2.39 of FTP 2023, what defines 'Merchanting Trade' carried out by an Indian trader?
OptionA: Sale of second-hand machinery within Special Economic Zones
OptionB: Wholesale retail trade in local vegetable mandis
OptionC: Shipment of goods from one foreign country to another foreign country without the goods entering Indian customs territory, involving an Indian intermediary and compliance with RBI guidelines
OptionD: Import of goods exclusively for free distribution
Explanation: Paragraph 2.39 permits Merchanting Trade where goods are procured from one foreign country and shipped directly to another foreign country without entering the domestic customs territory of India, subject to RBI guidelines. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 2.39)
CorrectText: Shipment of goods from one foreign country to another foreign country without the goods entering Indian customs territory, involving an Indian intermediary and compliance with RBI guidelines
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 2.39 - Merchanting Trade Criteria

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: How is the Export Obligation under an EPCG authorisation structured across the 6-year validity period under the Handbook of Procedures 2023?
OptionA: Block 1 (Years 1 to 4): Minimum 50% of total EO; Block 2 (Years 5 and 6): Remaining 50% of total EO
OptionB: No interim target; all 100% can be completed on the final day of the 6th year
OptionC: 100% must be fulfilled in the first year
OptionD: Equal 16.66% in each of the 6 years strictly
Explanation: Paragraph 5.12 of HBP 2023 mandates block-wise EO fulfillment: in the first block (1st to 4th year), at least 50% of total EO must be fulfilled, and in the second block (5th and 6th year), the balance 50% must be fulfilled. (Source: HBP 2023 Para 5.12)
CorrectText: Block 1 (Years 1 to 4): Minimum 50% of total EO; Block 2 (Years 5 and 6): Remaining 50% of total EO
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — FTP 2023 Para 5.04 - Block-wise EO Fulfillment

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Notification No. 11/2004-Customs, what is the duty-free concession granted to passengers importing a laptop computer (notebook computer)?
OptionA: Laptops are subject to 50% customs duty
OptionB: Up to five laptops can be imported duty-free by any child
OptionC: One laptop computer (notebook computer) imported by any passenger of age 18 years or above (other than crew member) is completely exempt from customs duty over and above the GFA
OptionD: Laptops can only be imported under an Advance Authorisation
Explanation: Notification No. 11/2004-Customs grants full exemption from basic customs duty and IGST to one laptop computer imported by any passenger of the age of 18 years or above (other than member of crew) in their baggage. (Source: Notif 11/2004-Cus / CBIC)
CorrectText: One laptop computer (notebook computer) imported by any passenger of age 18 years or above (other than crew member) is completely exempt from customs duty over and above the GFA
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Notification No. 11/2004-Customs - Laptop Exemption

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Section 80 of the Customs Act, 1962, what facility is provided to an incoming passenger carrying dutiable or prohibited baggage that they do not intend to clear into India?
OptionA: At the request of the passenger, the baggage may be detained by customs for the purpose of being returned to him when he leaves India
OptionB: The baggage is auctioned within 24 hours
OptionC: The baggage must be confiscated and destroyed immediately
OptionD: The passenger must pay double duty and forfeit the goods
Explanation: Section 80 provides that where the baggage of a passenger contains any article which is dutiable or prohibited, the proper officer may, at the request of the passenger, detain such article for the purpose of being returned to him on his leaving India. (Source: Section 80 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: At the request of the passenger, the baggage may be detained by customs for the purpose of being returned to him when he leaves India
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 80 - Temporary Detention of Baggage

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 74(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what percentage of import duty is refunded as drawback when imported goods are re-exported without being used in India?
Explanation: Section 74(1) provides that when goods capable of being easily identified which have been imported into India and upon which duties have been paid are exported without having been used in India, ninety-eight percent (98%) of such duty shall be repaid as drawback. (Source: Section 74(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: 98% of the import duty paid
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 74(1) - Unused Goods Re-Export Drawback

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 74(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Notification No. 19/65-Customs, what is the maximum period of use in India beyond which NO drawback is payable upon re-exportation?
Explanation: Under Notification No. 19/65-Customs as amended, where goods are used in India prior to re-export, the drawback percentage reduces in 3-month slabs down to 60% for 15-18 months; if the period of use exceeds 18 months, drawback is NIL. (Source: Notif 19/65-Cus / Section 74(2))
CorrectText: 18 months
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 74(2) - Drawback on Used Goods

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 75A(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, if duty drawback is not paid to the claimant within what statutory period from the date of filing the claim, must interest @ 6% per annum be paid to the claimant?
OptionB: One (1) month from the date of filing the claim
Explanation: Section 75A(1) provides that where any drawback payable to a claimant under Section 74 or 75 is not paid within a period of one month from the date of filing the claim, interest @ 6% per annum shall be payable to the claimant from the expiry of the said period of one month till payment. (Source: Section 75A(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: One (1) month from the date of filing the claim
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 75A - Interest on Delayed Drawback

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 76 of the Customs Act, 1962, under which of the following statutory conditions is the grant of duty drawback completely prohibited?
OptionA: If the goods are exported to a European nation
OptionB: In respect of any goods the market-price of which is less than the amount of drawback claimed, or where the drawback claim in respect of any shipment is less than fifty rupees (Rs 50)
OptionC: If the drawback claim is submitted electronically
OptionD: If the goods are shipped on an Indian flag vessel
Explanation: Section 76(1) bars drawback: (a) where market price is less than drawback amount, (b) where the drawback due on any single shipment is less than Rs 50, or (c) where goods are likely to be smuggled back into India. (Source: Section 76 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: In respect of any goods the market-price of which is less than the amount of drawback claimed, or where the drawback claim in respect of any shipment is less than fifty rupees (Rs 50)
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 76 - Prohibitions on Drawback Grant

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Section 20 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Notification No. 158/95-Customs, when Indian manufactured goods are exported and subsequently re-imported for repairs, what is the maximum permissible time frame within which the repaired goods must be re-exported back?
OptionB: 6 months (extendable up to one year by the Commissioner of Customs)
Explanation: Notification No. 158/95-Customs allows duty-free re-import of Indian goods for repairs or reconditioning on execution of a bond, subject to the condition that the goods are re-exported within 6 months (extendable up to one year by Commissioner). (Source: Notif 158/95-Cus / Section 20)
CorrectText: 6 months (extendable up to one year by the Commissioner of Customs)
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 20 / Notification No. 158/95-Customs

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Notification No. 45/2017-Customs, when goods exported under duty drawback or refund of IGST are re-imported into India without any alteration, what customs duty is payable upon re-importation?
OptionA: Full Basic Customs Duty and IGST as if the goods were originally manufactured abroad
OptionB: The amount of duty drawback or IGST refund availed at the time of export must be repaid, along with applicable interest
OptionD: Completely nil duty without any repayment
Explanation: Notification No. 45/2017-Customs prescribes that when goods exported under drawback, IGST refund, or duty exemption schemes are re-imported, the importer must repay the export incentive/drawback/refund availed at the time of export. (Source: Notif 45/2017-Cus / CBIC)
CorrectText: The amount of duty drawback or IGST refund availed at the time of export must be repaid, along with applicable interest
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Notification No. 45/2017-Customs

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015, what is the standard time limit within which full value of export goods must be realized and repatriated to India?
OptionA: Nine (9) months from the date of export (15 months in case of goods exported to a warehouse established outside India)
OptionC: 3 months from the date of export
Explanation: Regulation 9 of FEMA Export Regulations 2015 provides that the amount representing the full export value of goods shall be realized and repatriated to India within nine months from the date of export (or 15 months if exported to an overseas storage warehouse). (Source: RBI Master Direction - Export of Goods and Services)
CorrectText: Nine (9) months from the date of export (15 months in case of goods exported to a warehouse established outside India)
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Regulation 9 - Export Realization Time Period

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: What is the function of the EDPMS (Export Data Processing and Monitoring System) and IDPMS (Import Data Processing and Monitoring System) operated by the Reserve Bank of India in coordination with Customs?
OptionA: To track physical shipping container GPS coordinates in ocean waters
OptionB: To process tourist visa applications at airports
OptionC: To electronically reconcile customs shipping bills and bills of entry with inward and outward foreign exchange banking remittances, tracking unmatched payments and cautions
OptionD: To calculate personal income tax liabilities of port pilots
Explanation: EDPMS and IDPMS are RBI IT platforms integrated with ICEGATE to track and reconcile customs declarations (Shipping Bills and Bills of Entry) with actual cross-border inward and outward foreign exchange remittances processed by AD banks. (Source: RBI / CBIC Circulars)
CorrectText: To electronically reconcile customs shipping bills and bills of entry with inward and outward foreign exchange banking remittances, tracking unmatched payments and cautions
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — EDPMS and IDPMS Monitoring Systems

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under the Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017, what is the mandatory minimum remaining shelf-life required for imported food consignments at the time of customs import clearance?
OptionA: Not less than 60% of its original shelf-life (or three months, whichever is less) at the time of import clearance
OptionC: There is no shelf-life restriction for imported packaged foods
Explanation: Regulation 5(6) of FSSAI (Import) Regulations 2017 mandates that customs shall not clear any food consignment unless it has a valid remaining shelf-life of not less than 60% (or three months, whichever is less) at the time of clearance. (Source: FSSAI Import Regulations, 2017)
CorrectText: Not less than 60% of its original shelf-life (or three months, whichever is less) at the time of import clearance
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 5 - Minimum Remaining Shelf Life

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under the FSSAI (Import) Regulations, 2017, which of the following labeling deficiencies can be rectified by an importer inside a customs bonded warehouse prior to visual inspection and sampling?
OptionA: Affixing a single non-detachable sticker stating: Name and address of importer, FSSAI Logo and License Number, and Non-Veg/Veg Logo
OptionB: Altering the list of ingredients and country of origin
OptionC: Change of expiry date and nutritional value tables
OptionD: No labeling rectification is ever permitted in customs areas
Explanation: Under FSSAI guidelines and Regulation 6, rectifiable defects permitted to be corrected in customs bonded warehouses via a sticker are: (a) Importer name and address, (b) FSSAI logo and license number, and (c) Veg/Non-Veg logo. Core facts like expiry date and ingredients cannot be altered. (Source: FSSAI Order No. 1-1782/FSSAI/Imports/2018)
CorrectText: Affixing a single non-detachable sticker stating: Name and address of importer, FSSAI Logo and License Number, and Non-Veg/Veg Logo
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Regulation 6 - Rectifiable Labeling Defects

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, which mandatory declarations must be displayed on every pre-packaged commodity imported into India?
OptionA: The wholesale dealer price excluding GST
OptionB: The political affiliation of the overseas exporter
OptionC: Name and address of manufacturer and importer, generic name of commodity, net quantity in standard metric units, month and year of manufacture/import, Maximum Retail Price (MRP inclusive of all taxes), and consumer care contacts
OptionD: Only the name of the foreign shipping vessel
Explanation: Rule 6 of Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules 2011 mandates that all imported pre-packaged packages must display: importer name/address, generic name, net quantity, date of import/manufacture, Maximum Retail Price (MRP inclusive of all taxes), and customer helpline. (Source: Legal Metrology Rules, 2011 / CBIC Circular 33/2017-Cus)
CorrectText: Name and address of manufacturer and importer, generic name of commodity, net quantity in standard metric units, month and year of manufacture/import, Maximum Retail Price (MRP inclusive of all taxes), and consumer care contacts
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under the Plant Quarantine (Regulation of Import into India) Order, 2003, what official documentation is mandatory for import clearance of agricultural consignments and timber?
OptionA: An official Phytosanitary Certificate (PSC) issued by the National Plant Protection Organization (NPPO) of the exporting country certifying freedom from quarantine pests and weed seeds
OptionB: A Certificate of Fitness from the local municipal corporation
OptionC: A tourist brochure from the country of origin
Explanation: Under the PQ Order 2003, all agricultural seeds, plants, produce, and unprocessed wood/timber must be accompanied by an official Phytosanitary Certificate issued by the exporting country's NPPO and meet import permit phytosanitary conditions. (Source: PQ Order, 2003 / Directorate of Plant Protection)
CorrectText: An official Phytosanitary Certificate (PSC) issued by the National Plant Protection Organization (NPPO) of the exporting country certifying freedom from quarantine pests and weed seeds
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — PQ Order, 2003 - Phytosanitary Certificate

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Section: Rule 43A - Designated Ports of Import for Drugs
Question: Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, how is the import of bulk drugs and pharmaceutical formulations into India restricted geographically?
OptionA: Drugs can be unloaded at any dry dock without customs intervention
OptionB: Drugs can only enter through parcel post from neighboring countries
OptionC: Drugs can be imported through any minor private jetty across India
OptionD: Import of drugs is restricted strictly to designated notified customs ports, airports, and ICDs equipped with CDSCO Port Drug Control offices (e.g. Mumbai, Nhava Sheva, Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi)
Explanation: Rule 43A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 restricts the importation of drugs into India exclusively to notified ports and airports where CDSCO Assistant Drug Controllers are posted for inspection, verification of Form 10 import license, and NOC issuance. (Source: Rule 43A Drugs & Cosmetics Rules, 1945)
CorrectText: Import of drugs is restricted strictly to designated notified customs ports, airports, and ICDs equipped with CDSCO Port Drug Control offices (e.g. Mumbai, Nhava Sheva, Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi)
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 43A - Designated Ports of Import for Drugs

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under Rule 3 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what is the General Free Allowance (GFA) for an Indian resident or a foreigner residing in India arriving by air from countries other than Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar?
Explanation: Rule 3 of Baggage Rules 2016 provides that an Indian resident or foreigner residing in India arriving by air or sea from countries other than Nepal, Bhutan or Myanmar is entitled to a General Free Allowance (GFA) of Rs 50,000 for dutiable articles. (Source: Rule 3 Baggage Rules, 2016)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3 - General Free Allowance (GFA)

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Section: Rule 4 - Tourist of Foreign Origin GFA
Question: Under Rule 4 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what is the General Free Allowance permitted to a tourist of foreign origin arriving in India?
Explanation: Rule 4 of Baggage Rules 2016 provides that a tourist of foreign origin (other than from Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar) is entitled to clear used personal effects and travel souvenirs, plus other articles up to a value of Rs 15,000 duty-free. (Source: Rule 4 Baggage Rules, 2016)
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Rule 4 - Tourist of Foreign Origin GFA

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Rule 5 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what are the permissible duty-free jewellery allowances for a gentleman and a lady passenger respectively who have resided abroad for over one year?
OptionB: Gentleman: up to 20 grams with a value cap of Rs 50,000; Lady: up to 40 grams with a value cap of Rs 1,00,000
OptionD: Both are allowed up to 100 grams without any value ceiling
Explanation: Rule 5 provides that a passenger residing abroad for more than one year may bring duty-free jewellery: gentleman passenger up to 20 grams (value ceiling Rs 50,000); lady passenger up to 40 grams (value ceiling Rs 1,00,000). (Source: Rule 5 Baggage Rules, 2016)
CorrectText: Gentleman: up to 20 grams with a value cap of Rs 50,000; Lady: up to 40 grams with a value cap of Rs 1,00,000
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Rule 5 - Jewellery Allowance Limits

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Which of the following items is listed under Annexure I of Baggage Rules, 2016 and therefore CANNOT be imported under the General Free Allowance (GFA)?
OptionB: Firearms, cartridges exceeding 50, cigarettes exceeding 100 sticks, alcoholic liquor exceeding 2 litres, gold or silver in any form other than ornaments
Explanation: Annexure I items cannot be cleared under GFA: firearms, cartridges in excess of 50, cigarettes in excess of 100 or cigars in excess of 25 or tobacco in excess of 125g, alcoholic liquor/wines in excess of 2 litres, gold/silver in bars/bullion, and flat panel TVs. (Source: Annexure I Baggage Rules, 2016)
CorrectText: Firearms, cartridges exceeding 50, cigarettes exceeding 100 sticks, alcoholic liquor exceeding 2 litres, gold or silver in any form other than ornaments
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Annexure I - Non-GFA Dutiable Goods

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Section: Section 46(3) - Bill of Entry Filing Timeline
Question: Under Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962, by when must the importer present the Bill of Entry on the Common Portal?
OptionA: Before the end of the day (including holidays) preceding the day on which the aircraft or vessel or vehicle carrying the goods arrives at a customs station
OptionB: Only after the cargo has been unstuffed into a CFS
OptionC: Any time within one year from unloading
OptionD: Within 30 days after arrival of the ship
Explanation: Section 46(3) mandates that the importer shall present the bill of entry before the end of the day (including holidays) preceding the day on which the aircraft, vessel, or vehicle arrives at the customs station where goods are to be cleared. (Source: Section 46(3) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Before the end of the day (including holidays) preceding the day on which the aircraft or vessel or vehicle carrying the goods arrives at a customs station
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 46(3) - Bill of Entry Filing Timeline

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under Regulation 4 of the Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration and Paperless Processing) Regulations, 2018, what late fees are payable for delay in presenting the Bill of Entry?
OptionB: Rs 5,000 per day for the initial three days of default, and Rs 10,000 per day for each subsequent day of default
Explanation: Under the Bill of Entry Regulations 2018, late filing charges are prescribed as Rs 5,000 per day for the first three days of delay, and Rs 10,000 per day for each day thereafter until presentation of the bill of entry. (Source: Bill of Entry Regulations, 2018 / CBIC)
CorrectText: Rs 5,000 per day for the initial three days of default, and Rs 10,000 per day for each subsequent day of default
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Late Filing Charges

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: Under Section 47(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, within what time limit must the importer pay the assessed customs duty to avoid liability for interest under Section 28AA?
OptionA: Within 30 days of arrival of cargo
OptionB: Within 15 working days from grant of Out of Charge
OptionC: On the date of presentation of the bill of entry in the case of self-assessment, or within one day (excluding holidays) from the date on which the bill of entry is returned for payment of duty
Explanation: Section 47(2) provides that the importer shall pay the duty: (a) on the date of presentation in self-assessment, or (b) within one day (excluding holidays) from the date of return of bill of entry by the proper officer for payment; failing which interest @ 15% p.a. is payable. (Source: Section 47(2) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: On the date of presentation of the bill of entry in the case of self-assessment, or within one day (excluding holidays) from the date on which the bill of entry is returned for payment of duty
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 47(2) - Duty Payment Deadline

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: Under Section 17(5) of the Customs Act, 1962, where the proper officer re-assesses duty contrary to the self-assessment and the importer does not confirm acceptance in writing, within what period must the officer issue a speaking order?
OptionB: Within fifteen (15) days from the date of re-assessment of the bill of entry or the shipping bill
Explanation: Section 17(5) provides that where any re-assessment done under subsection (4) is contrary to the self-assessment and the importer/exporter has not confirmed acceptance in writing, the proper officer shall pass a speaking order within 15 days. (Source: Section 17(5) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Within fifteen (15) days from the date of re-assessment of the bill of entry or the shipping bill
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 17(5) - Speaking Order on Re-Assessment

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: Under Section 51 of the Customs Act, 1962, what statutory order must the proper officer make before export goods can be permitted to be loaded on a conveyance for exportation?
OptionA: No Objection Certificate from Port Trust
OptionB: Let Export Order (LEO) permitting clearance and loading of the goods
Explanation: Section 51 provides that where the proper officer is satisfied that goods are not prohibited and export duties/charges are paid, he shall make an order permitting clearance and loading of the goods for exportation, known as 'Let Export Order' (LEO). (Source: Section 51 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Let Export Order (LEO) permitting clearance and loading of the goods
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 51 - Let Export Order (LEO)

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: What is the primary role of a Turant Suvidha Kendra (TSK) established at Customs Stations under the Turant Customs / Faceless Assessment initiative?
OptionA: To conduct criminal interrogations of passengers
OptionC: To act as a single-point facilitation center for trade to submit physical documents, bonds, bank guarantees, debit bonds, and obtain physical prints without visiting multiple assessment groups
OptionD: To inspect physical cargo in shipping containers
Explanation: Turant Suvidha Kendras (TSK) were set up under Circular No. 28/2020-Customs as dedicated touchpoints at all customs ports to facilitate physical bond execution, bank guarantee debit/credit, and trade queries in a faceless environment. (Source: CBIC Circular 28/2020-Cus)
CorrectText: To act as a single-point facilitation center for trade to submit physical documents, bonds, bank guarantees, debit bonds, and obtain physical prints without visiting multiple assessment groups
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Turant Suvidha Kendra (TSK)

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: Under the e-SANCHIT (e-Storage and Computerized Handling of Indirect Tax documents) facility on ICEGATE, what is an 'IRN'?
OptionA: Image Reference Number, generated as a unique digital identifier upon uploading a supporting document in PDF format on e-SANCHIT, which is then tagged to the Bill of Entry
Explanation: On e-SANCHIT, when an importer or Customs Broker digitally signs and uploads a supporting document in PDF, the ICEGATE portal generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN), which is then linked in the Bill of Entry declaration. (Source: CBIC Circular 40/2017-Cus)
CorrectText: Image Reference Number, generated as a unique digital identifier upon uploading a supporting document in PDF format on e-SANCHIT, which is then tagged to the Bill of Entry
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Image Reference Number (IRN)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Question: Under Section 3(7) and 3(8) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, how is the value for the levy of Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) computed on imported goods?
OptionA: Retail Sale Price declared on the package
OptionC: Assessable Value under Section 14 PLUS Basic Customs Duty (BCD) PLUS any other applicable cesses (excluding IGST and GST Compensation Cess itself)
Explanation: Section 3(8) provides that the value of imported goods for levying IGST under subsection (7) shall be the aggregate of the assessable value determined under Section 14 and any duty of customs chargeable thereon (including BCD and SWS, but excluding IGST and Compensation Cess). (Source: Section 3(8) CTA 1975)
CorrectText: Assessable Value under Section 14 PLUS Basic Customs Duty (BCD) PLUS any other applicable cesses (excluding IGST and GST Compensation Cess itself)
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 3(7) - IGST Computation Base

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Question: Under Section 8B of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, on what statutory ground does the Central Government impose Safeguard Duty on an imported article?
OptionA: When any article is being imported into India in such increased quantities (absolute or relative to domestic production) and under such conditions as to cause or threaten to cause serious injury to domestic industry
OptionB: When the importer has failed to pay GST
OptionC: When the foreign exporter is selling goods below fair market value
OptionD: When the country of export devalues its national currency
Explanation: Section 8B(1) authorizes the Central Government to impose safeguard duty if satisfied that an article is being imported in increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic industry producing like or directly competitive articles. (Source: Section 8B CTA 1975)
CorrectText: When any article is being imported into India in such increased quantities (absolute or relative to domestic production) and under such conditions as to cause or threaten to cause serious injury to domestic industry
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 8B - Safeguard Duty

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Section: Section 9 - Countervailing Duty on Subsidized Goods
Question: Under Section 9 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, what is the maximum duration of a Countervailing Duty (CVD) imposed on subsidized articles imported into India?
OptionB: Five (5) years from the date of its imposition (subject to extension for a further 5 years upon a sunset review)
Explanation: Section 9(4) provides that countervailing duty on subsidized goods shall cease to have effect on the expiry of five years from the date of its imposition, unless extended for another period of five years following a review (sunset review). (Source: Section 9(4) CTA 1975)
CorrectText: Five (5) years from the date of its imposition (subject to extension for a further 5 years upon a sunset review)
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9 - Countervailing Duty on Subsidized Goods

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Question: Under Section 9A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, what is the statutory ceiling on the Anti-Dumping Duty that can be levied on dumped imported goods?
OptionA: The duty is fixed uniformly at USD 100 per metric ton
OptionB: The duty shall not exceed the margin of dumping in relation to such article (Margin of Dumping = Normal Value in exporting country minus Export Price to India)
OptionC: The duty cannot exceed 25% of CIF value
OptionD: The duty cannot exceed the total ocean freight
Explanation: Section 9A(1) prescribes that the anti-dumping duty imposed shall not exceed the margin of dumping determined in relation to the article, where margin of dumping is the difference between normal value and export price. (Source: Section 9A CTA 1975)
CorrectText: The duty shall not exceed the margin of dumping in relation to such article (Margin of Dumping = Normal Value in exporting country minus Export Price to India)
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9A - Anti-Dumping Duty (ADD)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Section: Section 9C - Appeal to CESTAT against ADD/CVD
Question: Under Section 9C of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, within what time limit must an appeal against an order of determination or review of Anti-Dumping Duty or Countervailing Duty be filed before CESTAT?
OptionA: Ninety (90) days from the date of the order under appeal
Explanation: Section 9C(2) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 provides that an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal against an order of determination regarding existence, degree, and effect of dumping or subsidy shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order. (Source: Section 9C CTA 1975)
CorrectText: Ninety (90) days from the date of the order under appeal
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9C - Appeal to CESTAT against ADD/CVD

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Question: Under Section 110 of the Finance Act, 2018, how is the Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) calculated on imported goods?
OptionB: 10% of the total CIF value of the shipment
OptionC: Flat Rs 500 per Bill of Entry
OptionD: Ten percent (10%) calculated on the aggregate of duties, taxes, and cesses levied under Section 12 of the Customs Act (specifically Basic Customs Duty), excluding IGST and Compensation Cess
Explanation: Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) is levied @ 10% on the aggregate of customs duties (primarily Basic Customs Duty). It is NOT levied on Integrated Tax (IGST) or GST Compensation Cess. (Source: Section 110 Finance Act, 2018 / CBIC Circular)
CorrectText: Ten percent (10%) calculated on the aggregate of duties, taxes, and cesses levied under Section 12 of the Customs Act (specifically Basic Customs Duty), excluding IGST and Compensation Cess
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1962, when is an importer NOT liable to pay customs duty on pilfered goods?
OptionA: If the goods were insured under a marine policy
OptionB: Only if the thief is convicted by a criminal court
OptionC: If goods are pilfered at any time within 5 years after clearance
OptionD: If any imported goods are pilfered after the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse, and the goods are not restored to the importer
Explanation: Section 13 provides that if imported goods are pilfered after unloading and before an order for clearance for home consumption or warehousing is made, the importer shall not be liable to pay the duty thereon unless the goods are restored. (Source: Section 13 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: If any imported goods are pilfered after the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse, and the goods are not restored to the importer
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 13 - Pilfered Goods

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 22 of the Customs Act, 1962, how is the customs duty determined on imported goods that have sustained damage or deterioration before or during unloading?
OptionA: Full duty must be paid without any deduction
OptionB: Goods are exempt from all duty unconditionally
OptionC: Duty is replaced by a flat port storage fee
OptionD: Duty is charged proportionately to the diminished value, calculated as duty on undamaged value multiplied by the ratio of damaged value to undamaged value
Explanation: Section 22(1) allows abatement of duty on goods damaged/deteriorated before or during unloading, or in warehouse before clearance; duty chargeable is reduced in proportion to the diminution in value determined by the proper officer. (Source: Section 22 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Duty is charged proportionately to the diminished value, calculated as duty on undamaged value multiplied by the ratio of damaged value to undamaged value
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 22 - Abatement on Damaged Goods

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 23(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the statutory provision regarding duty on goods lost or destroyed before clearance?
OptionA: Duty is refunded only after an inquiry by the Supreme Court
OptionB: Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs that any imported goods have been lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption, the officer shall remit the duty
OptionC: The shipping line is arrested automatically
OptionD: The importer must pay double duty as penalty
Explanation: Section 23(1) mandates remission of duty where goods are lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed by accidental fire, flood, or natural cause at any time before clearance for home consumption. (Source: Section 23(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs that any imported goods have been lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption, the officer shall remit the duty
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 23(1) - Goods Lost or Destroyed

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 23(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, up to what point can the owner of imported goods relinquish title to the goods to avoid paying customs duty?
OptionA: Relinquishment of title is barred under Indian law
OptionB: At any time before an order for clearance of goods for home consumption under Section 47 or an order for permitting deposit of goods in a warehouse under Section 60 has been made, provided no offence has been committed
OptionC: Only before the ship arrives in Indian territorial waters
OptionD: At any time within three years after clearing the goods home
Explanation: Section 23(2) allows the owner to relinquish his title to the goods at any time before an order for clearance under Section 47 or deposit in a warehouse under Section 60 is made, and thereupon he shall not be liable to pay duty (proviso bars relinquishment if offence is committed). (Source: Section 23(2) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: At any time before an order for clearance of goods for home consumption under Section 47 or an order for permitting deposit of goods in a warehouse under Section 60 has been made, provided no offence has been committed
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 23(2) - Relinquishment of Title

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 27(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the statutory time limit for an importer or exporter to make an application for refund of duty and interest to the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs?
OptionA: One (1) year from the date of payment of duty and interest (or date of final assessment in case of provisional assessment)
Explanation: Section 27(1) provides that any person claiming refund of duty or interest shall make an application within one year from the date of payment of such duty or interest, or from the date of adjustment of duty after final assessment under Section 18. Explanation: Regulation 5 requires the applicant to be a citizen of India, graduate, possess professional qualification (CA/MBA/LLB/CS/ICWA etc.), and furnish a CA certificate of financial viability showing net worth of at least Rs 5 Lakhs. (Source: Regulation 5 CBLR, 2018)

OptionD: Authorizations can be obtained orally via phone call
Explanation: Regulation 10(a) mandates that a Customs Broker shall obtain an authorization from each client by whom he is employed and produce such authorization to the proper officer whenever required. (Source: Regulation 10(a) CBLR, 2018)

Explanation: Regulation 10(d) requires the Customs Broker to advise the client to comply with the Act and rules, and if the client fails to do so, bring such non-compliance to the notice of the Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs. (Source: Regulation 10(d) CBLR, 2018)

Question: Under Regulation 10(l) of CBLR, 2018, what is the statutory duty of a Customs Broker regarding money received from a client for duty payment?
