Section: Section 108 - Legal Nature of Summons Proceedings
Question: Under Section 108(4) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the legal character of an inquiry proceeding before a Gazetted Officer of Customs where a person is summoned to give evidence or produce documents?
OptionA: It is equivalent to an arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act
OptionB: It is a confidential commercial mediation
OptionC: It is deemed to be a 'judicial proceeding' within the meaning of Section 193 and Section 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)
OptionD: It is an informal administrative inquiry with no legal consequences
Explanation: Section 108(4) explicitly provides that every inquiry under Section 108 shall be deemed to be a 'judicial proceeding' within the meaning of Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code, making intentional false statements punishable as perjury. (Source: Section 108(4) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: It is deemed to be a 'judicial proceeding' within the meaning of Section 193 and Section 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: How do statements recorded under Section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962 differ from statements recorded by police officers under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)?
OptionB: Section 108 statements can only be used if signed by three independent witnesses
OptionC: A statement recorded under Section 108 before a Gazetted Officer of Customs is substantive admissible evidence in judicial proceedings, as customs officers are not police officers under Section 25 of the Evidence Act
OptionD: Statements under Section 108 are completely inadmissible in court
Explanation: The Supreme Court has consistently held that customs officers are not 'police officers' within the meaning of Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act; therefore, voluntary statements recorded under Section 108 are admissible evidence in trial. (Source: Ramesh Chandra Mehta v. State of WB / Section 108)
CorrectText: A statement recorded under Section 108 before a Gazetted Officer of Customs is substantive admissible evidence in judicial proceedings, as customs officers are not police officers under Section 25 of the Evidence Act
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 108 - Admissibility of Confessional Statements

Question: Under Section 103 of the Customs Act, 1962, what statutory procedure must be followed if an officer has reason to believe that a person has smuggled goods (such as gold or narcotics) secreted inside their body?
OptionA: The person must be produced before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay, and only with the Magistrate's order may the person's body be screened or X-rayed by a qualified medical practitioner
OptionB: Body screening is prohibited under customs law
OptionC: The officer can immediately perform surgery on the spot
OptionD: The person must be kept in lockup for 14 days without medical advice
Explanation: Section 103 mandates that if an officer believes a person has secreted goods inside their body, the person must be produced before a Magistrate, who alone has the power to direct that the person be screened or X-rayed by a registered medical practitioner. (Source: Section 103 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The person must be produced before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay, and only with the Magistrate's order may the person's body be screened or X-rayed by a qualified medical practitioner
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 103 - Power to Screen Body of Suspected Person

OptionD: Delivering cargo within 24 hours to reduce port dwell time

CorrectText: Authorizing an officer to allow an illicit or suspect consignment of goods to pass into, through or out of India under customs supervision with a view to identifying persons involved in smuggling or illicit trafficking

OptionD: Whenever cargo is transported by Indian Railways

Question: Under Section 147(3) of the Customs Act, 1962, when is an agent (such as a Customs Broker) deemed to be personally liable for customs duty or penalties in respect of goods transacted on behalf of a principal?
OptionA: When any person is expressly or impliedly authorized by the owner, importer, or exporter to be his agent in respect of such goods, any duty, penalties, or charges recoverable from the owner may be recovered from the agent if not recovered from the owner, unless the agent proves that he acted diligently without knowledge of wrongdoing
OptionB: The agent must surrender all personal real estate
OptionC: The agent is never liable under any circumstances
OptionD: The agent is liable for 100 times the value of the goods
Explanation: Section 147(3) provides that any duty, penalty, or charges leviable on the principal may be recovered from the agent as if he were the owner, subject to statutory safeguards where the agent acted without fault or knowledge of misdeclaration. (Source: Section 147(3) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: When any person is expressly or impliedly authorized by the owner, importer, or exporter to be his agent in respect of such goods, any duty, penalties, or charges recoverable from the owner may be recovered from the agent if not recovered from the owner, unless the agent proves that he acted diligently without knowledge of wrongdoing

OptionD: A Chartered Accountant holding a valid Certificate of Practice

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 151A of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the statutory LIMITATION placed on the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) when issuing orders, instructions, or directions to customs officers?
OptionA: The Board shall NOT issue orders, instructions, or directions requiring any customs officer to make a particular assessment or dispose of a particular case in a particular manner, nor interfere with the discretion of the Commissioner (Appeals)
OptionB: CBIC instructions can only be issued in Hindi
OptionC: CBIC cannot issue any instructions on holidays
OptionD: CBIC cannot alter the uniform of customs officers
Explanation: The provisos to Section 151A strictly prohibit the Board from issuing directions requiring any customs officer to make a specific assessment or decide a particular case in a particular manner, thereby preserving quasi-judicial independence. (Source: Section 151A Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: The Board shall NOT issue orders, instructions, or directions requiring any customs officer to make a particular assessment or dispose of a particular case in a particular manner, nor interfere with the discretion of the Commissioner (Appeals)
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 151A - CBIC Instructions to Officers

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Section: Section 153 - Modes of Service of Orders & Decisions
Question: Under Section 153(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, which of the following is a recognized legal mode of serving any order, decision, summons, or notice on a person?
OptionB: Only through physical publication in the Gazette of India
OptionC: Sending a message via social media messenger without verification
OptionD: By tender/hand delivery, registered/speed post, email to the registered email address, making it available on the Common Portal (ICEGATE), or publication in a newspaper/notice board
Explanation: Section 153(1) outlines statutory service modes: (a) physical delivery, (b) registered/speed post/courier, (c) registered email, (d) making available on the Common Customs Electronic Portal, and (e) affixture on notice board/newspaper publication. (Source: Section 153(1) Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: By tender/hand delivery, registered/speed post, email to the registered email address, making it available on the Common Portal (ICEGATE), or publication in a newspaper/notice board
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 153 - Modes of Service of Orders & Decisions

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Section: Section 143 - Power to Allow Importation on Execution of Bond
Question: Under Section 143 of the Customs Act, 1962, when may the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner of Customs permit the clearance of goods without production of required documents or compliance with certain formalities?
OptionA: Clearance without documents is strictly prohibited under all circumstances
OptionB: Upon execution by the importer of a bond with such surety or security as the officer deems fit, binding the importer to produce the documents or fulfill the conditions within a specified time limit
OptionC: Without any bond if the shipment value is below Rs 1 Crore
OptionD: Only upon payment of cash bribe to the dock worker
Explanation: Section 143 empowers the proper officer to permit clearance of goods pending production of required documents or fulfillment of conditions, upon execution of a bond with appropriate surety/security binding compliance within the allowed period. (Source: Section 143 Customs Act, 1962)
CorrectText: Upon execution by the importer of a bond with such surety or security as the officer deems fit, binding the importer to produce the documents or fulfill the conditions within a specified time limit
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 143 - Power to Allow Importation on Execution of Bond

Chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
Question: Under the three-tier AEO Programme for importers and exporters, what percentage of bank guarantee is waived for an entity holding AEO-T2 status?
OptionD: No waiver is granted; only fast-track clearance is provided
Explanation: Under CBIC Circular No. 33/2016-Customs as amended, AEO-T1 holders enjoy a 50% bank guarantee waiver, while AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 entities enjoy a 100% bank guarantee waiver wherever bank guarantees are statutorily required.
CorrectText: 100% waiver (full exemption from bank guarantee)
Topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — CBIC Circular No. 33/2016-Customs

Chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
Question: What is the statutory validity period of an AEO Certificate issued to an entity under AEO-T1 and AEO-T2 tiers?
OptionB: 5 years for both AEO-T1 and AEO-T2
OptionC: 3 years for both AEO-T1 and AEO-T2
OptionD: 1 year for T1 and 2 years for T2
Explanation: Under the AEO Programme (Circular 33/2016-Cus), certificates for AEO-T1 and AEO-T2 are valid for 3 years, whereas certificates for AEO-T3 and AEO-LO (Logistics Operators/Customs Brokers) are valid for 5 years.
CorrectText: 3 years for both AEO-T1 and AEO-T2
Topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Regulation 6 / Circular 33/2016

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Section: Section 47(1) Proviso & Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016
Question: Under the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016, which category of importers is eligible to avail the benefit of deferred payment of customs duty?
OptionA: Entities certified as AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 tier status holders
OptionB: Any importer who has filed more than 100 Bills of Entry in a financial year
Explanation: Under the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016 read with Section 47(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, deferred payment facility is extended strictly to approved classes of importers, namely AEO Tier-2 and Tier-3 certified entities.
CorrectText: Entities certified as AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 tier status holders
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 47(1) Proviso & Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Section: Rule 5, Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016
Question: Under Rule 5 of the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016, by what date must customs duty be paid for goods cleared between the 1st and 15th day of any month (except March)?
OptionA: By the last day of the same month
OptionB: By the 5th day of the succeeding month
OptionC: By the 20th day of the same month
OptionD: By the 16th or 17th day of the same month
Explanation: Under Rule 5 of Deferred Payment Rules 2016, for bills of entry returned between 1st to 15th of a month, duty must be paid by the 16th (or 17th if ECL mode). For 16th to end of month, by 1st of next month; and for 16th to 31st March, by 31st March.
CorrectText: By the 16th or 17th day of the same month
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 5, Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under the proviso to Section 149 of the Customs Act, 1962, an amendment to a Bill of Entry after goods have been cleared for home consumption may be allowed only if:
OptionA: A formal recommendation is issued by the DGFT
OptionB: The differential duty involved does not exceed Rs. 1 Lakh
OptionC: The importer pays a mandatory compounding penalty of Rs. 25,000
OptionD: The amendment is based on documentary evidence which was in existence at the time the goods were cleared
Explanation: The proviso to Section 149 explicitly mandates that no amendment of a Bill of Entry or Shipping Bill shall be allowed after clearance, unless the amendment is substantiated by documentary evidence which was already in existence at the time the goods were cleared, deposited in a warehouse, or exported.
CorrectText: The amendment is based on documentary evidence which was in existence at the time the goods were cleared
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 149 Proviso

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 128(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the limitation period for filing an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), and what is the maximum condonable period?
OptionB: 90 days, with no statutory power of condonation
OptionC: 60 days, condonable by further 30 days on sufficient cause
Explanation: Section 128(1) mandates that an appeal to Commissioner (Appeals) must be filed within 60 days from the date of communication of the decision/order. The Commissioner (Appeals) may allow a further period of 30 days if satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause.
CorrectText: 60 days, condonable by further 30 days on sufficient cause
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 128(1)

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 129E of the Customs Act, 1962, what percentage of the duty demanded or penalty imposed must be pre-deposited before filing an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals)?
Explanation: Under Section 129E(i), an appeal before Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 128 cannot be entertained unless the appellant has pre-deposited 7.5% of the duty demanded or penalty imposed (subject to a maximum ceiling of Rs. 10 Crores).
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129E(i)

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: What is the mandatory pre-deposit percentage required under Section 129E(iii) when appealing to the CESTAT against an order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals)?
Explanation: Under Section 129E(iii), for filing an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) against an order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals), the appellant must deposit 10% of the duty demanded or penalty imposed, capped at Rs. 10 Crores.
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129E(iii)

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under the first proviso to Section 129A(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, which of the following matters is expressly barred from being heard by the CESTAT?
OptionB: Confiscation of gold and precious metals exceeding Rs. 50 Lakhs
OptionC: Orders passed by Commissioner (Appeals) relating to baggage, short-landing in transit, and drawback
OptionD: Valuation disputes under the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007
Explanation: The first proviso to Section 129A(1) bars CESTAT from hearing appeals against orders of Commissioner (Appeals) relating to: (a) any goods imported/exported as baggage, (b) goods loaded in a conveyance for import but short-landed, and (c) payment of drawback. These disputes lie exclusively by Revision Application to the Central Government under Section 129DD.
CorrectText: Orders passed by Commissioner (Appeals) relating to baggage, short-landing in transit, and drawback
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129A(1) First Proviso

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 129DD of the Customs Act, 1962, a Revision Application to the Central Government against an order of the Commissioner (Appeals) must be filed within what period?
OptionB: 6 months from the date of the order
OptionD: 3 months from date of communication (extendable by further 3 months)
Explanation: Under Section 129DD(2), an application for revision must be made within 3 months from the date of communication of the order. The Central Government may extend this period by a further 3 months if satisfied there was sufficient cause.
CorrectText: 3 months from date of communication (extendable by further 3 months)
Topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129DD

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 104 of the Customs Act, 1962, an offence is categorized as cognizable and non-bailable only if the duty evasion, fraudulent drawback, or value of prohibited goods exceeds:
Explanation: Under Section 104(4) & (6) as amended, customs offences are non-cognizable and bailable, EXCEPT where the market price of prohibited goods or evasion of duty/fraudulent drawback exceeds Rs. 50 Lakhs (or specified unauthorized importation/exportation exceeds Rs. 1 Crore), in which case they become cognizable and non-bailable.
CorrectText: Rs. 50 Lakhs
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 104(4) & (6)

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 135(1)(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, for an offence involving duty evasion exceeding Rs. 50 Lakhs, the offender is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to:
OptionD: 7 years and with fine (with a minimum sentence of 1 year in the absence of special reasons)
Explanation: Section 135(1)(i) prescribes imprisonment up to 7 years and fine for duty evasion or fraudulent drawback exceeding Rs. 50 Lakhs (or relating to prohibited goods). In the absence of special and adequate reasons recorded in the judgment, the imprisonment shall not be for less than 1 year.
CorrectText: 7 years and with fine (with a minimum sentence of 1 year in the absence of special reasons)
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 135(1)(i)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Where the proper officer re-assesses duty under Section 17(4) contrary to self-assessment, within how many days must a speaking order be passed if the importer has not confirmed acceptance in writing?
OptionB: 30 days from the date of re-assessment
OptionD: 15 days from the date of re-assessment
Explanation: Under Section 17(5) of the Customs Act, 1962, where any re-assessment done under sub-section (4) is contrary to the self-assessment and the importer/exporter does not confirm acceptance in writing, the proper officer shall pass a speaking order within 15 days from the date of re-assessment of the bill of entry or the shipping bill.
CorrectText: 15 days from the date of re-assessment
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 17(5)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: When a provisional duty assessment is finalized under Section 18(2) and the importer is liable to pay differential duty, from which date is interest payable under Section 18(3)?
OptionA: From the first day of the month in which duty was provisionally assessed till the date of payment
OptionB: From 3 months after the provisional assessment date
OptionC: From the date of filing the original Bill of Entry
OptionD: From the date of the final assessment order
Explanation: Section 18(3) mandates that the importer shall be liable to pay interest on any differential duty from the first day of the month in which duty was provisionally assessed till the date of payment thereof, at the rate fixed under Section 28AA (currently 15% p.a.).
CorrectText: From the first day of the month in which duty was provisionally assessed till the date of payment
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 18(3)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Section: Section 18(1A) & Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regs, 2018
Question: Under the Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2018, what is the primary time limit within which a provisional assessment must be finalized by the proper officer?
OptionB: 6 months from the date of provisional assessment
OptionC: 1 year from the date of provisional assessment
OptionD: 2 years from the date of provisional assessment (extendable by Commissioner by 1 year)
Explanation: Under Section 18(1A) and the 2018 Regulations, provisional assessment must be finalized within 2 years from the date of provisional assessment. The Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs may extend this period by a further period not exceeding 1 year on sufficient cause shown.
CorrectText: 2 years from the date of provisional assessment (extendable by Commissioner by 1 year)
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 18(1A) & Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regs, 2018

Chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
Question: Under the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, for what minimum duration is an auditee required to preserve and maintain all customs-related books of accounts, records, and electronic data?
OptionB: 5 years from the date of clearance of goods
OptionD: 3 years from end of the financial year
Explanation: Regulation 3 of the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018 mandates that an auditee shall preserve and maintain all records, books of account, and data related to customs transactions for a minimum period of 5 years from the date of clearance of goods.
CorrectText: 5 years from the date of clearance of goods
Topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Section 99A & Customs Audit Regulations, 2018

Chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
Question: Before conducting a Premises-Based Audit (PBA) at the business premises of an auditee under Section 99A, what is the minimum advance notice required to be served by the proper officer?
OptionD: No notice is required; surprise visits are statutory
Explanation: Under Regulation 4(1) of the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, the proper officer shall give not less than 15 days advance notice in writing to the auditee before conducting an audit at their premises.
CorrectText: At least 15 days advance notice
Topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Regulation 4, Customs Audit Regulations, 2018

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Section: Section 46(3) & Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration) Regs, 2018
Question: Under Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 read with CBIC regulations, what are the prescribed late charges for delay in presenting a Bill of Entry?
OptionA: Rs. 5,000 per day for the initial 3 days, and Rs. 10,000 per day for each subsequent day
OptionB: Rs. 2,500 per day up to 7 days, and Rs. 5,000 thereafter
OptionC: Flat Rs. 10,000 irrespective of the number of days
OptionD: Rs. 1,000 per day for all days of delay
Explanation: Under Section 46(3) and Notification No. 36/2018-Customs (N.T.), late filing fees are levied at Rs. 5,000 per day for the first 3 days of delay following the arrival deadline, and Rs. 10,000 per day for each subsequent day of delay.
CorrectText: Rs. 5,000 per day for the initial 3 days, and Rs. 10,000 per day for each subsequent day
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 46(3) & Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration) Regs, 2018

Chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
Question: Under the second proviso to Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962, an advance or prior Bill of Entry may be presented up to how many days before the expected arrival of the vessel or aircraft?
Explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 (as amended by Finance Act 2018 and Notification 36/2018-Cus), a Bill of Entry may be presented at any time not exceeding 30 days prior to the expected arrival of the vessel or aircraft.
CorrectText: 30 days
Topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 46(3) Second Proviso

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Section 48 of the Customs Act, 1962, if imported goods are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused within what statutory timeframe from unloading, may the custodian proceed to sell them after giving notice?
Explanation: Section 48 provides that if any goods brought into India from outside are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused within 30 days from the date of unloading (or such extended time as allowed by the proper officer), the custodian may, with customs permission, sell them after giving notice to the importer.
CorrectText: 30 days
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 48

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 6(4) of CBLR 2018, a candidate is permitted a maximum of how many attempts within what period from the date of application?
OptionB: Unlimited attempts until the age of 50 years
Explanation: Under Regulation 6(4) of CBLR 2018, the applicant shall be allowed a maximum of 6 attempts within a period of 7 years from the date of application to clear both the written and oral examinations.
CorrectText: 6 attempts within 7 years
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 6(4)

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 7(2) of CBLR 2018, a Customs Broker license granted in Form B is valid for a period of:
OptionA: Lifetime validity with annual renewal fees
OptionC: 10 years (renewable for 10 years at a time)
Explanation: Under Regulation 7(2) of the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018, a license granted under Regulation 7 shall be valid for a period of 10 years from the date of issue, and may be renewed for further periods of 10 years at a time.
CorrectText: 10 years (renewable for 10 years at a time)
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 7(2)

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 10(n) of CBLR 2018, what is the mandatory obligation of a Customs Broker regarding client verification?
OptionA: Obtain a simple signed letter on the client's letterhead
OptionB: Request a police verification certificate prior to taking up customs work
OptionC: Conduct a physical site inspection with two local witnesses and a notary
OptionD: Verify the correctness of IEC, identity of client, and functioning of client at declared address using reliable, independent source documents
Explanation: Regulation 10(n) mandates that a Customs Broker shall verify the correctness of the Importer Exporter Code (IEC) number, identity of client and functioning of client at the declared address by using reliable, independent, authentic documents, data or information (KYC norms).
CorrectText: Verify the correctness of IEC, identity of client, and functioning of client at declared address using reliable, independent source documents
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10(n)

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 13 of CBLR 2018, what is the functional difference between a 'G-card' holder and an 'H-card' holder?
OptionA: G-card holders handle ocean customs; H-card holders handle air customs
OptionB: G-card holders have passed the Reg 13 exam and can sign declarations; H-card holders are non-exam clerks who assist and cannot sign declarations
OptionC: G-card holders are permanent partners; H-card holders are temporary apprentices
OptionD: There is no functional difference; they denote different customs ports
Explanation: Under Regulation 13, employees who qualify the examination under Regulation 13 are issued a 'G-card' authorising them to sign customs declarations. Other non-qualified assistants are issued an 'H-card' valid for assisting in movement and examination of cargo without authority to sign legal customs declarations.
CorrectText: G-card holders have passed the Reg 13 exam and can sign declarations; H-card holders are non-exam clerks who assist and cannot sign declarations
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 13(1), (5) & (6)

Chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
Question: Under Regulation 18 of the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018, what is the maximum penalty that a Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs may impose on a Customs Broker for contravention of any provision?
Explanation: Regulation 18 of CBLR 2018 provides that the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs may impose a penalty not exceeding Rs. 50,000 on a Customs Broker who contravenes any of the provisions of these regulations.
Topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 18

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under General Rule of Interpretation 2(a), how is an incomplete or unfinished article classified if presented unassembled or disassembled (CKD/SKD)?
OptionA: Classified under the heading appearing last in numerical order
OptionB: Classified as parts and accessories under their respective headings
OptionC: Classified as the complete or finished article, provided it has the essential character of the complete article
OptionD: Classified under the residual heading of Chapter 98 as project cargo
Explanation: GIR 2(a) states: 'Any reference in a heading to an article shall be taken to include a reference to that article incomplete or unfinished, provided that, as presented, the incomplete or unfinished article has the essential character of the complete or finished article. It shall also be taken to include a reference to that article complete or finished ... presented unassembled or disassembled.'
CorrectText: Classified as the complete or finished article, provided it has the essential character of the complete article
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 2(a)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under GIR 3(a), when goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, the rule of preference dictates that:
OptionA: The heading carrying the highest duty rate shall always be applied
OptionB: The heading providing the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description
OptionC: The importer may freely select whichever heading carries the lowest rate of duty
OptionD: The heading carrying the lower numerical code takes automatic precedence
Explanation: GIR 3(a) provides: 'The heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description.' However, when two or more headings each refer to part only of materials, those headings are regarded as equally specific.
CorrectText: The heading providing the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 3(a)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under GIR 3(b), composite goods consisting of different materials or goods put up in sets for retail sale are classified based on:
OptionA: The component that is mentioned first in the commercial packing list
OptionB: The component that represents more than 50% of the total invoice value
OptionC: The heading that carries the lowest basic customs duty
OptionD: The component which gives them their essential character
Explanation: GIR 3(b) explicitly provides that mixtures, composite goods consisting of different materials or made up of different components, and goods put up in sets for retail sale, which cannot be classified by reference to 3(a), shall be classified as if they consisted of the material or component which gives them their essential character.
CorrectText: The component which gives them their essential character
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 3(b)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: When goods cannot be classified by reference to Rule 3(a) or 3(b), how are they classified under Rule 3(c)?
OptionA: Under the residual 'Other' code of Chapter 99
OptionB: Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
OptionC: By statutory determination of the Settlement Commission
OptionD: Under the heading occurring first in numerical order among those meriting consideration
Explanation: GIR 3(c) states: 'When goods cannot be classified by reference to (a) or (b), they shall be classified under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration.'
CorrectText: Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 3(c)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under GIR 5(a), camera cases, musical instrument cases, and specially shaped containers entered with the articles they are intended to contain are classified:
OptionA: Free of duty as non-dutiable packaging assists
OptionB: With such articles, if they are of a kind normally sold therewith and suitable for long-term use, unless the container gives the whole its essential character
OptionC: Always separately under Chapter 42 as articles of leather/plastics
Explanation: GIR 5(a) provides that cases shaped or fitted to contain a specific article or set of articles, suitable for long-term use and presented with the articles for which they are intended, shall be classified with such articles when of a kind normally sold therewith. This rule does not apply to containers giving the whole its essential character.
CorrectText: With such articles, if they are of a kind normally sold therewith and suitable for long-term use, unless the container gives the whole its essential character
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 5(a)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: What is the normal limitation period for the proper officer to issue a Show Cause Notice for non-levy, short-levy, or erroneous refund of customs duty under Section 28(1) in the absence of fraud or collusion?
OptionD: 3 years from the end of the financial year
Explanation: Under Section 28(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 (as amended by Finance Act 2016), the normal limitation period for issuing a notice for duty not levied, short-levied, or erroneously refunded is 2 years from the relevant date.
CorrectText: 2 years from the relevant date
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(1)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 28(4) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the limitation period for demanding duty where non-levy or short-levy is by reason of collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts?
OptionA: 10 years from the date of clearance
Explanation: Section 28(4) provides that where duty has not been levied, has been short-levied or erroneously refunded by reason of collusion, any wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts by the importer or exporter, the limitation period to issue a notice is 5 years from the relevant date.
CorrectText: 5 years from the relevant date
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(4)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 28(5) of the Customs Act, 1962, if an assessee pays the duty demanded under Section 28(4) along with interest within 30 days of receipt of the notice, what is the reduced penalty payable?
Explanation: Under Section 28(5) of the Customs Act, 1962, where the duty specified in the notice under sub-section (4) is paid along with interest within 30 days of the receipt of the notice, the penalty payable shall be 15% of the duty, and all proceedings in respect of the said duty and interest shall be deemed to be concluded.
CorrectText: 15% of the duty amount
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(5)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 74(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what percentage of import duty paid is admissible as drawback when duty-paid imported goods are entered for export without having been used in India?
Explanation: Under Section 74(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, when goods capable of being easily identified which have been imported into India and upon which duties have been paid are exported without having been used, 98% of such duty shall be repaid as drawback.
CorrectText: 98% of duty paid
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 74(1)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Notification No. 19/65-Customs as amended, what is the maximum period of use of goods in India beyond which drawback under Section 74 is completely nil?
Explanation: Under Section 74(2) read with Notification No. 19/65-Customs as amended, drawback on imported goods used before re-export is progressively reduced, and is explicitly NIL if the period between the date of clearance for home consumption and the date of export exceeds 36 months (3 years).
CorrectText: 36 months (3 years)
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 74(2) & Notification 19/65-Customs

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Section 76(1)(c) of the Customs Act, 1962, no drawback shall be allowed in respect of any goods if the amount of drawback claimed is less than:
Explanation: Section 76(1)(c) of the Customs Act, 1962 provides that no drawback shall be allowed in respect of any goods where the amount of drawback in respect of any single claim is less than Rs. 50.
CorrectText: Rs. 50
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 76(1)(c)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017, an application for determination of Brand Rate of duty drawback must be filed within what timeframe from the date of export (LEO)?
OptionA: 3 months (extendable by a further 3 months on payment of fee)
OptionC: 1 year from the date of shipping bill
Explanation: Under Rule 6(1) and Rule 7(1) of the Drawback Rules 2017, the manufacturer-exporter must apply for Brand Rate fixation within 3 months from the relevant export date. The Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs may extend this period by a further 3 months on sufficient cause and payment of prescribed late fee.
CorrectText: 3 months (extendable by a further 3 months on payment of fee)
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Rule 6 & Rule 7

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 110 of the Finance Act, 2018, what is the rate of Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) levied on imported goods, and on what value is it calculated?
OptionB: 10% calculated on the assessable CIF value of the goods
OptionC: 4% calculated on basic customs duty plus IGST
OptionD: 10% calculated on the aggregate of all duties of customs levied under Section 12 (excluding IGST and Compensation Cess)
Explanation: Section 110 of the Finance Act, 2018 levies Social Welfare Surcharge at 10% on the aggregate duties of customs levied under Section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962. It is not calculated on assessable value, and IGST under Sec 3(7) and Compensation Cess under Sec 3(9) of CTA 1975 are statutorily excluded from the SWS base.
CorrectText: 10% calculated on the aggregate of all duties of customs levied under Section 12 (excluding IGST and Compensation Cess)
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 110, Finance Act, 2018

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Question: Under Section 9A(5) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, for how long does an Anti-Dumping Duty remain in force from the date of its imposition, unless revoked earlier?
Explanation: Under Section 9A(5) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, Anti-Dumping Duty ceases to have effect on the expiry of 5 years from the date of its imposition. If the Central Government initiates a sunset review before the expiry, the duty may remain in force pending review for a period up to 1 year.
CorrectText: 5 years (unless extended upon sunset review)
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9A(5)

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
Question: Under Section 9A(2) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, what is the maximum duration for which a provisional Anti-Dumping Duty may be imposed pending final determination?
OptionC: 6 months (extendable to 9 months by Central Government upon request)
Explanation: Section 9A(2) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 provides that provisional anti-dumping duty shall remain in force for a period not exceeding 6 months, which may, upon request of exporters representing a significant percentage of trade, be extended by the Central Government to 9 months.
CorrectText: 6 months (extendable to 9 months by Central Government upon request)
Topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9A(2)

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
Question: Under Para 5.01 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023, what is the Export Obligation (EO) requirement under the zero-duty EPCG scheme for imported capital goods?
OptionA: 6 times the duty saved on capital goods, to be fulfilled in 6 years from authorization date
OptionB: Equal to the CIF value of imported capital goods within 3 years
OptionC: 10 times the duty saved in 8 years
OptionD: 8 times the FOB value within 5 years
Explanation: Under Para 5.01 of FTP 2023, import of capital goods for pre-production, production, and post-production is allowed at zero customs duty under the EPCG Scheme subject to an Export Obligation equivalent to 6 times the duty saved on capital goods, to be fulfilled within 6 years from authorization date.
CorrectText: 6 times the duty saved on capital goods, to be fulfilled in 6 years from authorization date
Topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Para 5.01, Foreign Trade Policy 2023

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Para 4.08 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023, what is the minimum mandatory Value Addition required for exports under an Advance Authorization (except for tea)?
Explanation: Para 4.08 of FTP 2023 stipulates that a minimum 15% value addition shall be required for issuance of an Advance Authorization, except for export of tea where the minimum value addition requirement is 50%.
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Para 4.08, Foreign Trade Policy 2023

Act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
Chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
Question: Under Para 1.25 of FTP 2023, what is the export performance threshold (in USD equivalent) required to obtain 'One Star Export House' status?
Explanation: Under FTP 2023 Para 1.25, the thresholds in US Dollars FOB/FOR during current and previous three financial years are: One Star = $3 Million, Two Star = $15 Million, Three Star = $50 Million, Four Star = $200 Million, Five Star = $800 Million.
CorrectText: USD 3 Million
Topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Para 1.25, Foreign Trade Policy 2023

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: Under Notification No. 19/2023-Customs (N.T.), which of the following categories of import goods is EXEMPTED from the mandatory payment of customs duties through the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL)?
OptionA: Commercial containers cleared through inland container depots (ICDs)
OptionB: Goods imported under the EPCG scheme
OptionC: Goods imported through courier or postal channels, and passenger baggage
Explanation: Notification No. 19/2023-Customs (N.T.) specifically exempts passenger baggage, goods imported/exported through international courier or postal routes, and non-EDI manual bills from the mandatory ECL mechanism under Section 51A.
CorrectText: Goods imported through courier or postal channels, and passenger baggage
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 51A & Notification No. 19/2023-Customs (N.T.)

Act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
Chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
Question: Under the e-SANCHIT paperless customs initiative, what document identifier is generated when a supporting document is successfully uploaded by an authorized signatory using digital signature?
OptionB: Goods and Services Tax Identification Number (GSTIN)
Explanation: Under e-SANCHIT (Circular 40/2017-Cus), when an importer or Customs Broker uploads a digitally signed PDF supporting document on ICEGATE, the system validates the digital signature and generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN), which is then quoted in the Bill of Entry.
CorrectText: Image Reference Number (IRN)
Topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — CBIC Circular No. 40/2017-Customs

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: In a High Sea Sale transaction where goods are sold prior to customs clearance, on what value is customs duty assessed on the ultimate high sea buyer?
OptionA: The original foreign supplier invoice value paid by the first importer
OptionB: The final high sea sale value paid by the ultimate buyer (including high sea sales margin/commission)
OptionC: The average of the original invoice price and high sea sales invoice price
OptionD: The minimum tariff value notified by DGFT
Explanation: In high sea sales, the actual transaction value under Section 14 is the price paid by the final buyer who files the Bill of Entry for home consumption, which encompasses the original CIF cost plus the high sea seller's mark-up/commission (Circular No. 32/2004-Cus).
CorrectText: The final high sea sale value paid by the ultimate buyer (including high sea sales margin/commission)
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Section 14 & CBIC Circular No. 32/2004-Cus

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Rule 6 of the IGCR Rules, 2022, by which date of each succeeding month must an importer submit the monthly statement in Form IGCR-3 on the common portal?
OptionA: By the last day of the succeeding quarter
OptionB: By the 20th day of the succeeding month
OptionC: By the 10th day of the succeeding month
OptionD: By the 5th day of the succeeding month
Explanation: Rule 6(1) of the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022 requires the importer to submit a monthly statement in Form IGCR-3 electronically on the common portal by the 10th day of the following month.
CorrectText: By the 10th day of the succeeding month
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 6, IGCR Rules 2022

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under Rule 7(1) of the IPR (Imported Goods) Enforcement Rules, 2007, once the proper officer suspends clearance of suspected counterfeit goods, within how many days must the right holder join proceedings?
OptionB: 10 working days for normal goods, and 3 working days for perishable goods
OptionD: 3 working days for normal goods, 24 hours for perishables
Explanation: Under Rule 7(1) of IPR Rules 2007, the right holder shall join the proceedings within a period of 10 working days (or 3 working days in the case of perishable goods) from the date of notice of suspension of clearance, failing which the goods are released to the importer.
CorrectText: 10 working days for normal goods, and 3 working days for perishable goods
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 7(1)

Chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
Question: Under Rule 9 of the IPR Enforcement Rules, 2007, can counterfeit trademark goods or pirated copyright goods be released to the importer on payment of a redemption fine?
OptionA: Yes, provided the brand owner receives 50% of the auction proceeds
OptionB: Yes, upon payment of double the standard redemption fine under Section 125
OptionC: No; counterfeit goods cannot be released into commercial channels even with consent, and must be destroyed or disposed of outside commerce
OptionD: Yes, if the counterfeit marks are erased with customs permission
Explanation: Rule 9 explicitly prohibits the release of infringing goods to the importer upon payment of fine or duty, and prohibits re-exportation in unaltered state. Counterfeit goods must be destroyed or disposed of outside channels of commerce under customs supervision.
CorrectText: No; counterfeit goods cannot be released into commercial channels even with consent, and must be destroyed or disposed of outside commerce
Topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 9

Act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
Chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
Question: Under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, pre-packaged commodities imported into India are EXEMPT from retail MRP labeling declarations if:
OptionA: The packages are meant strictly for industrial consumers or institutional consumers
OptionB: The goods are cleared through an Inland Container Depot (ICD)
OptionC: The goods originate from SAARC preferential trade countries
OptionD: The goods are packaged in containers of less than 100 grams
Explanation: Under Rule 3 of the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, packages intended for industrial consumers (who buy directly for manufacturing) or institutional consumers (hospitals, railways, hotels) are exempt from Chapter II retail declarations including MRP.
CorrectText: The packages are meant strictly for industrial consumers or institutional consumers
Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3, Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under the first proviso to Section 114A of the Customs Act, 1962, where an equal penalty is imposed for collusion, willful misstatement or suppression under Section 114A:
OptionA: A parallel penalty under Section 112 or Section 114 shall also be levied mandatorily
OptionB: The Commissioner must obtain CESTAT approval before recovery
OptionC: No penalty shall be imposed on the person under Section 112 or Section 114
OptionD: The prosecution under Section 135 is automatically barred
Explanation: The first proviso to Section 114A explicitly bars double jeopardy by providing that where penalty is imposed under Section 114A, no penalty under Section 112 (improper importation) or Section 114 (improper exportation) shall be imposed on the same person for the same offence.
CorrectText: No penalty shall be imposed on the person under Section 112 or Section 114
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114A First Proviso

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 114AA of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the maximum penalty for intentionally using a false or incorrect declaration, statement, or forged document in customs business?
OptionC: Up to equal to the duty evaded
OptionD: Up to five times the value of the goods
Explanation: Section 114AA provides that if any person intentionally makes, signs or uses any declaration, statement or document which is false or incorrect in any material particular, he shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five times the value of the goods.
CorrectText: Up to five times the value of the goods
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114AA

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 125(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the statutory ceiling on the fine that may be imposed in lieu of confiscation (redemption fine)?
OptionA: The assessable CIF value of the goods
OptionC: Double the amount of basic customs duty
OptionD: The market price of the goods confiscated, less the duty chargeable thereon
Explanation: The proviso to Section 125(1) mandates that the fine in lieu of confiscation shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less in the case of imported goods the duty chargeable thereon.
CorrectText: The market price of the goods confiscated, less the duty chargeable thereon
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 125(1) Proviso

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
Question: Under Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1962, an importer is NOT liable to pay customs duty on pilfered goods, provided the pilferage occurred:
OptionA: Before the bill of lading was endorsed by the shipping line
OptionB: At any time while the goods are lying in a public bonded warehouse
OptionC: After the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or warehousing
OptionD: While the vessel was carrying goods on the high seas
Explanation: Section 13 provides that if any imported goods are pilfered after the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse, the importer shall not be liable to pay duty. Once out-of-charge or in-bond order is made, Section 13 does not apply.
CorrectText: After the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or warehousing
Topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 13

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 23(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner shall remit duty on imported goods if it is proved that the goods have been lost or destroyed:
OptionA: At any time before clearance for home consumption, including while in a customs warehouse
OptionB: Only before the goods are unloaded from the ship
OptionC: Only if the loss is due to enemy action or war
OptionD: Only after filing a formal insurance subrogation claim
Explanation: Section 23(1) applies to goods lost (other than as a result of pilferage) or destroyed by accident at ANY time before clearance for home consumption, including while warehoused under Chapter IX. Duty on such goods shall be remitted by the proper officer.
CorrectText: At any time before clearance for home consumption, including while in a customs warehouse
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 23(1)

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under the proviso to Section 23(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, an owner of imported goods is PROHIBITED from relinquishing title to the goods if:
OptionA: The goods are packaged in wooden crates
OptionB: Any offence appears to have been committed under this Act or any other law in respect of such goods
OptionC: The goods have been lying uncleared for more than 15 days
OptionD: The assessable value of the consignment exceeds Rs. 10 Lakhs
Explanation: The proviso to Section 23(2) clearly states: 'Provided that the owner of any such imported goods shall not be allowed to relinquish his title to such goods regarding which an offence appears to have been committed under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.'
CorrectText: Any offence appears to have been committed under this Act or any other law in respect of such goods
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 23(2) Proviso

Chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
Question: Under Section 27(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, what is the limitation period for an importer to claim a refund of customs duty, and where is the refund credited if unjust enrichment is not rebutted?
OptionA: 6 months; credited to the Consolidated Fund of India
OptionB: 2 years; refunded to the shipping agent
OptionC: 1 year from date of payment; credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund under Section 12C of Central Excise Act
OptionD: 3 years; credited to the Port Trust Authority
Explanation: Section 27(1) prescribes 1 year limitation from payment date. Under Section 27(2), the refund is statutorily credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund established under Section 12C of the Central Excise Act, 1944, unless the applicant proves that the incidence of duty had not been passed on to any other person.
CorrectText: 1 year from date of payment; credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund under Section 12C of Central Excise Act
Topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 27(1) & (2)

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 102(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, when an officer is about to search any person under Section 100 or 101, what statutory right must the officer inform the person of?
OptionA: The right to be taken without unnecessary delay to the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate
OptionB: The right to call a legal practitioner immediately
OptionC: The right to conduct self-search in the presence of a doctor
OptionD: The right to refuse search until a judicial warrant is produced
Explanation: Section 102(1) mandates that when an officer of customs is about to search any person under Section 100 or 101, he shall, if such person so requires, take him without unnecessary delay to the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate.
CorrectText: The right to be taken without unnecessary delay to the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 102(1)

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 108(4) of the Customs Act, 1962, every inquiry conducted by an officer summoning a person is deemed to be a:
OptionA: Summary trial before a Sessions Court
OptionB: Confidential departmental inquiry without legal consequence
OptionC: Commercial dispute subject to the Arbitration and Conciliation Act
OptionD: Judicial proceeding within the meaning of Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)
Explanation: Section 108(4) provides that every inquiry under Section 108 shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 and section 228 of the Indian Penal Code. Giving false evidence or refusing to answer is punishable as perjury.
CorrectText: Judicial proceeding within the meaning of Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 108(4)

Chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
Question: Under Section 110A of the Customs Act, 1962, who is the authority empowered to order provisional release of any goods seized under Section 110 pending adjudication?
OptionA: The Adjudicating Authority, on taking a bond from the owner with such security and conditions as may be required
OptionB: The High Court having territorial jurisdiction
Explanation: Section 110A provides that any goods, documents or things seized under Section 110 may, pending the order of the adjudicating authority, be released to the owner upon taking a bond from him in the proper form with such security and conditions as the adjudicating authority may require.
CorrectText: The Adjudicating Authority, on taking a bond from the owner with such security and conditions as may be required
Topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 110A

Chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
Question: Under Section 127B(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, an application for settlement of a case can be made only if the additional amount of duty accepted by the applicant exceeds:
Explanation: Under Section 127B(1) first proviso, no application shall be made unless the applicant has filed a bill of entry or shipping bill, received a show cause notice, and the additional amount of duty accepted by the applicant in his application exceeds three lakh rupees.

Question: Under Section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, when any goods are removed from a Special Economic Zone to the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA), what duties are chargeable?
OptionA: Customs duties including Basic Customs Duty, IGST, anti-dumping duty and countervailing duty, as if imported into India
OptionB: Nil duty, as both are situated within the geographical boundaries of India
OptionC: A flat compounding tax of 5% on factory gate value
OptionD: Only Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST)
Explanation: Under Section 30 of the SEZ Act, 2005, any goods removed from an SEZ to the DTA shall be chargeable to duties of customs, including basic customs duty, integrated tax, compensation cess and anti-dumping duty, at the rate in force on the date of removal.

OptionB: Cannot exceed 20% of the FOB value of the goods

OptionD: Actual air freight regardless of amount

Topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2) Third Proviso
